[P5633|Heading 1] Traffic Managemant Configuration Guide
[P5634|Heading 2] Configuring QoS
[P5635|Heading 3] Overview
[P5636|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P5637|Normal] Quality of Service (QoS) can be used to give certain traffic priority over other traffic. Without QoS, all traffic in a network has the same priority and chance of being delivered on time. If congestion occurs, all traffic has the same chance of being dropped. With QoS, specific network traffic can be prioritized to receive preferential treatment. In turn, a network performs more predictably, and utilizes bandwidth more effectively.
[P5638|Body Text] Classification information can be carried in the Layer-3 IP packet header or the Layer-2 frame. IP packet headers carry the information using 6 bits or 3 bits from the deprecated IP type of service (TOS) field. Layer-2 802.1Q frames carry the information using a 2-byte Tag Control Information field.
[P5639|Body Text] All switches and routers accessing the Internet depend on class information to give the same forwarding treatment to packets with the same class information, and give different treatment to packets with different class information. A packet can be assigned class information, as follows:
[P5640|Item List] End hosts or switches along a path, based on a configured policy
[P5641|Item List] Detailed packet examination, expected to occur nearer to the network edge, to prevent overloading core switches and routers
[P5642|Item List] A combination of the above two techniques
[P5643|Normal] Class information can be used by switches and routers along a path to limit the amount of allotted resources per traffic class.
[P5644|Body Text] Per-hop behavior is an individual device’s behavior when handling traffic in the DiffServ architecture. An end-to-end QoS solution can be created if all devices along a path have consistent per-hop behavior.
[P5645|Body Text] QoS (Quality of Service) provides different service qualities to different requirements for all kinds of applications. For example, providing specified bandwidth, reducing the rate of lost for packets, and reducing the delay time and delay variation. To reach the goals, QoS often using different techniques to realize, for instance, traffic classification and tinting, traffic policing, traffic shaping, administrate network congestion, and avoid network congestion and so on. They will do as the following:
[P5646|Item List] Traffic classification: According to certain match regulations to recognized objects.
[P5647|Item List] Traffic policing: it will supervise the specification of certain traffic which entering the network equipments. When the traffic exceeds the specification, it will take actions of limitation or punishments, to protect the service provider’s business profits and network resources from damages.
[P5648|Item List] Traffic shaping: it is a kind of traffic control that adjusts the output of speed rate actively. Usually it is used for adapting downstream router that provides network resources, and avoids unnecessary packets discard and congestion.
[P5649|Item List] Administrate network congestion: it is the actions that when network jam happens and needs to solve the resource competition. It usually put the packets into queue buffer, and uses some kinds of scheduling algorithm to arrange the order of forwarding packets.
[P5650|Item List] Avoid network congestion: excessive congestion will cost damages for network resource; network congestion will avoid the usage of network resource. When it detects that the congestion has a trend of rapidly growth, it will take actions to discard packets, which terminates the network overload by adjusting traffic.
[P5651|Normal] Among these QoS techniques, traffic classification is the fundamental one, it will recognize packets by certain regulations and it is the precondition of operating QoS; the rest of these techniques are detailed expression of QoS by controlling network traffic and resources from different aspects.
[P5652|Body Text] 
[P5653|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P5654|Heading 5] 1.Brief description of terms and concepts used to describe QoS
[P5655|Heading 5] ACL
[P5656|Normal] Access control lists (ACLs) classify traffic with the same characteristics. IP traffic is classified using IP ACLs, and non-IP traffic is classified using MAC ACLs. The ACL can have multiple access control entries (ACEs), which are commands that match fields against the contents of the packet.
[P5657|Heading 5] CoS Value
[P5658|Normal] Class of Service (CoS) is a 3-bit value used to classify the priority of Layer-2 frames upon entry into a network.
[P5659|Body Text] QoS classifies frames by assigning priority-indexed CoS values to them, and gives preference to higher-priority traffic.
[P5660|Body Text] Layer-2 802.1Q frame headers have a 2-byte Tag Control Information field that carries the CoS values in the 3 most significant bits, called the User Priority bits. On interfaces configured as Layer-2 802.1Q trunks, all traffic is in 802.1Q frames, except for traffic in the native VLAN.
[P5661|Body Text] Other frame types cannot carry Layer-2 CoS values. CoS values range from 0 to 7.
[P5662|Heading 5] DSCP Value
[P5663|Normal] Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) is a 6-bit value used to classify the priority of Layer-3 packets upon entry into a network.
[P5664|Body Text] DSCP values range from 0 to 63.
[P5665|Heading 5] IP-Precedence Value
[P5666|Normal] IP-Precedence is a 3-bit value used to classify the priority of Layer-3 packets upon entry into a network.
[P5667|Body Text] IP-Precedence values range from 0 to 7.
[P5668|Heading 5] EXP Value
[P5669|Normal] EXP value is a 3-bit value used to classify the priority of MPLS packets upon entry into a network.
[P5670|Body Text] MPLS EXP values range from 0 to 7.
[P5671|Heading 5] Classification
[P5672|Normal] Classification distinguishes one kind of traffic from another by examining the fields in the packet. The process generates an internal priority for a packet, which identifies all future QoS actions to be taken on the packet.
[P5673|Body Text] Each packet is classified upon entry into the network. At the ingress, the packet is inspected, and the priority is determined based on ACLs or the configuration. The Layer-2 CoS value is then mapped to a priority value.
[P5674|Body Text] The classification is carried in the IP packet header using 6 bits or 3 bits from the deprecated IP TOS field to carry the classification information. Classification can also occur in the Layer-2 frame.
[P5675|Body Text] Classification occurs on an ingress physical port, but not at the switch virtual interface level.
[P5676|Body Text] Classification can be based on CoS/inner-CoS/DSCP/IP-Precedence, default port cos, or class maps and policy maps.
[P5677|Heading 5] Shaping
[P5678|Normal] Shaping is to change the rate of incoming traffic flow to regulate the rate in such a way that the outgoing traffic flow behaves more smoothly. If the incoming traffic is highly bursty, it needs to be buffered so that the output of the buffer is less bursty and smoother.
[P5679|Body Text] Shaping has the following attributes:
[P5680|Item List] Shaping can be deployed base on physical port.
[P5681|Item List] Shaping can be deployed on queues of egress interface.
[P5682|Heading 5] Policing
[P5683|Normal] Policing determines whether a packet is in or out of profile by comparing the internal priority to the configured policer.
[P5684|Body Text] The policer limits the bandwidth consumed by a traffic flow. The result is given to the marker.
[P5685|Body Text] There are two types of policers:
[P5686|Item List] Individual: QoS applies the bandwidth limits specified in the policer, separately, to each matched traffic class. An individual policer is configured within a policy map.
[P5687|Item List] Aggregate: QoS applies the bandwidth limits specified in an aggregate policer, cumulatively, to all matched traffic flows. An aggregate policer is configured by specifying the policer name within a policy map. The bandwidth limits of the policer are specified. In this way, the aggregate policer is shared by multiple classes of traffic within one or multiple policy map.
[P5688|Heading 5] Marking
[P5689|Normal] Marking determines how to handle a packet when it is out of profile. It assesses the policer and the configuration information to determine the action required for the packet, and then handles the packet using one of the following methods:
[P5690|Item List] Let the packet through and mark color down
[P5691|Item List] Drop the packet
[P5692|Normal] Marking can occur on ingress and egress interfaces.
[P5693|Heading 5] Queuing
[P5694|Normal] Queuing maps packets to a queue. Each egress port can accommodate up to 8 unicast queues, 1 multicast queue and 1 SPAN queue.
[P5695|Body Text] The packet internal priority can be mapped to one of the egress queues. The unit of queue depth is buffer cell. Buffer cell is the granularity, which is 288 bytes, for packet storing.
[P5696|Body Text] After the packets are mapped to a queue, they are scheduled.
[P5697|Heading 5] Tail Drop
[P5698|Normal] Tail drop is the default congestion-avoidance technique on the interface. With tail drop, packets are queued until the thresholds are exceeded. The packets with different priority and color are assigned to different drop precedence. The mapping between priority and color to queue and drop precedence is configurable. You can modify the three tail-drop threshold to every egress queue by using the queue threshold interface configuration command. Each threshold value is packet buffer cell.
[P5699|Heading 5] WRED
[P5700|Normal] Weighted Random Early Detection (WRED) differs from other congestion-avoidance techniques because it attempts to anticipate and avoid congestion, rather than controlling congestion when it occurs.
[P5701|Body Text] WRED reduces the chances of tail drop by selectively dropping packets when the output interface begins to show signs of congestion. By dropping some packets early rather than waiting until the queue is full, WRED avoids dropping large numbers of packets at once. Thus, WRED allows the transmission line to be fully used at all times. WRED also drops more packets from large users than small. Therefore, sources that generate the most traffic are more likely to be slowed down versus sources that generate little traffic.
[P5702|Body Text] You can enable WRED and configure the two thresholds for a drop-precedence assigned to every egress queues. The WRED’s color drop precedence map is the same as tail-drop’s. Each min-threshold represents where WRED starts to randomly drop packets. After min-threshold is exceeded, WRED randomly begins to drop packets assigned to this threshold. As the queue max-threshold is approached, WRED continues to drop packets randomly with the rate of drop-probability. When the max-threshold is reached, WRED drops all packets assigned to the threshold. By default, WRED is disabled.
[P5703|Heading 5] Scheduling
[P5704|Normal] Scheduling forwards conditions packets using combination of WDRR and SP. Every queue belongs to a class. The class range from 0 to 7, and 7 is the highest priority. Several queues can be in a same class, or non queue in some class. Packets are scheduled by SP between classes and WDRR between queues in a class.
[P5705|Item List] Strict Priority-Based (SP), in which any high-priority packets are first transmitted. Lower-priority packets are transmitted only when the higher-priority queues are empty. A problem may occur when too many lower-priority packets are not transmitted.
[P5706|Item List] Weighted Deficit Round Robin (WDRR), in which each queue is assigned a weight to control the number of packets relatively sent from each queue.
[P5707|Heading 5] Class Map
[P5708|Normal] A class map names and isolates specific traffic from other traffic. The class map defines the criteria used to match against a specific traffic flow to further classify it. The criteria can match several access groups defined by the ACL.
[P5709|Body Text] If there is more than one type of traffic to be classified, another class map can be created under a different name. After a packet is matched against the class-map criteria, it is further classified using a policy map.
[P5710|Heading 5] Policy Map
[P5711|Normal] A policy map specifies on which traffic class to act. This can be implemented as follows:
[P5712|Item List] Set a specific priority and color in the traffic class.
[P5713|Item List] Set a specific trust policy to map priority and color.
[P5714|Item List] Specify the traffic bandwidth limitations for each matched traffic class (policer) and the action to take (marking) when the traffic is out of profile.
[P5715|Item List] Redirect the matched traffic class to a specific physical interface.
[P5716|Item List] Mirror the matched traffic class to a specific monitor session, which’s destination is defined in mirror module(please refer to the “monitor session destination” command).
[P5717|Item List] Enable statistics of matching each ace or each class-map(if the class-map operator is match-any).
[P5718|Item List] Policy maps have the following attributes:
[P5719|Item List] A policy map can contain multiple class statements, each with different match criteria and action.
[P5720|Item List] A separate policy-map class can exist for each type of traffic received through an interface.
[P5721|Item List] There can be only one policy map per interface per direction. The same policy map can be applied to multiple interfaces and directions.
[P5722|Item List] Before a policy map can be effective, it must be attached to an interface.
[P5723|Item List] A policy map can be applied on physical interface(not link agg member), link agg interface, or vlan interface.
[P5724|Heading 5] Mapping Tables
[P5725|Normal] During QoS processing, the switch represents the priority of all traffic (including non-IP traffic) with an internal priority value:
[P5726|Item List] During classification, QoS uses configurable mapping tables to derive the internal priority (a 6-bit value) from received CoS, EXP(3-bit), DSCP or IP precedence (3-bit) values. These maps include the CoS-to-priority-color/COS-to-PHB map, EXP-to-priority-color/EXP-to-PHB map, DSCP-to-priority-color/DSCP-to-PHB map and the IP-precedence-to- priority-color/IP-PREC-to-PHB map.
[P5727|Item List] During policing, QoS can assign another priority and color to an IP or non-IP packet (if the packet matches the class-map). This configurable map is called the policed-priority-color map.
[P5728|Item List] Before the traffic reaches the scheduling stage, and replace CoS or DSCP is set, QoS uses the configurable priority-color-to-CoS or priority-color-to-DSCP map to derive a CoS or DSCP value from the internal priority color.
[P5729|Item List] Each QoS domain has an independent set of map tables mentioned above.
[P5730|Heading 5] Time-range
[P5731|Normal] By using time-range, the aces in the class-map can be applied based on the time of day or week. First, define a time-range name and set the times and the dates or the days of the week in the time range. Then enter the time-range name when adding an ace. You can use the time-range to define when the aces in the class-map are in effect, for example, during a specified time period or on specified days of the week.
[P5732|Body Text] These are some of the many possible benefits of using time-range:
[P5733|Item List] You can control over permitting or denying a user access to resources, such as an application, which is identified by an IP address and a port number.
[P5734|Item List] You can obtain the traffic statistics during appointed time.
[P5735|Item List] You can define when the action of a traffic class is in effect.
[P5736|Heading 5] SRTCM
[P5737|Normal] Single Rate Three Color Marker
[P5738|Heading 5] TRTCM
[P5739|Normal] Two Rate Three Color Marker
[P5740|Heading 5] CIR
[P5741|Normal] Committed Information Rate
[P5742|Heading 5] CBS
[P5743|Normal] Committed Burst Size
[P5744|Heading 5] EIR
[P5745|Normal] Excess Information Rate
[P5746|Heading 5] EBS
[P5747|Normal] Excess Burst Size
[P5748|Heading 5] PIR
[P5749|Normal] Peak Information Rate
[P5750|Heading 5] PBS
[P5751|Normal] Peak Burst Size
[P5752|Heading 5] Modular QoS CLI
[P5753|Normal] Input traffic is classified to a specified traffic class. All qos policies are attached to this traffic class.
[P5754|Heading 5] class-map type qos
[P5755|Normal] Type qos of class-map is used to identify traffic. The identification rules can be CoS/DSCP/IP Precendence/EXP/ACL.
[P5756|Heading 5] policy-map type qos
[P5757|Normal] Type qos of policy-map is used to assign traffic class. Type qos of class-map is refered by same type of policy-map.
[P5758|Heading 5] class-map type traffic-class
[P5759|Normal] Type traffic-class of class-map is used to identify traffic class. The identification rules is traffic class value.
[P5760|Heading 5] policy-map type traffic-class
[P5761|Normal] Type traffic-class of policy-map is used to specify qos policies. Type traffic-class of class-map is refered by same type of policy-map.
[P5762|Heading 5] 2. Brief description of terms and concepts used to describe MQC
[P5763|Normal] Switch provides much simpler MQC (Modular QoS CLI) configuration patterns than the original one. The network administrators will not need to care about how to solve with the message import or export separately. They only need to configure aim at the policy map, and then apply policy map to certain interface. It reduces the requirements for network administrators and maintainers.
[P5764|Body Text] class map and policy map:
[P5765|Item List] Class-map: it is used for matching message and queue, and then using the results into certain policy-map to continue for next step.
[P5766|Item List] Policy-map: it is used to define a group of class-map class set, and it will set up corresponding policy for each class.
[P5767|Normal] Class-map and policy-map has two types each:
[P5768|Item List] qos: it is used for techniques of traffic classification, traffic policing, associated queue and re-mark priority level and will used for the inbound of packets.
[P5769|Item List] Traffic-class: it is the related operations of setting queue, for example, traffic shaping, discard policy, schedule priority and weight.
[P5770|Normal] The process of system MQC configuration is:
[P5771|Item List] Configure class-map type qos matches the message, it can be COS, DSCP, IP-Precedence or ACL.
[P5772|Item List] Apply class-map type qos into policy-map type qos. For different class-map, set up different relevant queue, traffic policing, re-mark and other operations. Those traffic classifications which do not match will classify by class-default, default associated queue 0 and cannot be setup with WDRR scheduling weight. This policy map will apply into the inbound of message.
[P5773|Item List] Configure class-map type traffic-class matching queue, support configure queue 1 to 7, 0 is reserved for system and cannot be configured by user.
[P5774|Item List] Apply class-map type traffic-class into policy-map type traffic-class. For different class-map, they set up different traffic shaping, discards type, schedule priority, weighted factor and so on. Class-default has the default value which is marked with queue 0; it does not provide operations that setting WDRR schedule weight. This policy map will apply into outbound of packets
[P5775|Normal] 
[P5776|Item List] The same policy-map can apply to multiple interfaces.
[P5777|Item List] The same interface only can apply to one ingress policy-map (policy-map type qos) and one egress policy-map (policy-map type traffic-class) at the same time.
[P5778|Heading 3] Configuration
[P5779|Normal] The following provides information to consider before configuring QoS:
[P5780|Item List] QoS policing cannot be configured on Linkagg interface.
[P5781|Item List] Traffic can be only classified per ingress port.
[P5782|Item List] There can be multiple ACLs per class map. An ACL can have multiple access control entries that match fields against the packet contents.
[P5783|Item List] Policing cannot be done at the switch virtual interface level.
[P5784|Normal] To configure a QoS policy, the following is usually required:
[P5785|Item List] Categorize traffic into classes.
[P5786|Item List] Configure policies to apply to the traffic classes.
[P5787|Item List] Attach policies to interfaces.
[P5788|Heading 4] Classify Traffic Using ACLs
[P5789|Normal] IP traffic can be classified using IP ACLs. The following shows creating an IP ACL for IP traffic. Follow these steps from Privileged Exec mode.
[P5790|Item List] configure terminal.
[P5791|Item List] ip access-list ACCESS-LIST-NAME. ACCESS-LIST-NAME = name of IP ACL
[P5792|Item List] create ACEs, Repeat this step as needed. For detail, please refer to ACL configuration Guide
[P5793|Normal] The no ip access-list command deletes an access list.
[P5794|Body Text] The following example shows allowing access only for hosts on three specified networks. Wildcard bits correspond to the network address host portions. If a host has a source address that does not match the access list statements, it is rejected.
[P5795|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P5796|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5797|Heading 5] step 2 Create ACL and ACEs
[P5798|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip access-list ip-acl
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any 128.88.12.0 0.0.0.255 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any 28.88.0.0 0.0.255.255 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any 11.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# exit
[P5799|Normal] Use the “no ip access-list” in global configure mode to remove the ACL. Use the “no sequence-num” in ACL configure mode to remove the ACE.
[P5800|Body Text] Terminology:
[P5801|Item List] ACL：Access Control List
[P5802|Item List] ACE：Access Control Entry
[P5803|Heading 5] step 3 Exit the configure mode
[P5804|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5805|Heading 5] step 4 Validation
[P5806|Terminal Display] Switch# show access-list ip ip-acl
ip access-list ip-acl
  10 permit any 128.88.12.0 0.0.0.255 any 
  20 permit any 28.88.0.0 0.0.255.255 any 
  30 permit any 11.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 any
[P5807|Heading 4] Create class-map
[P5808|Normal] The following shows classifying IP traffic on a physical-port basis using class maps. This involves creating a class map, and defining the match criterion. In this case it is configuring a class map named cmap1 with 1 match criterion: IP access list ip-acl, which allows traffic from any source to any destination.
[P5809|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P5810|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5811|Heading 5] step 2 Create ACL and ACEs
[P5812|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip access-list ip-acl
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any any any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# quit
[P5813|Heading 5] step 3 Create class-map and match the ACL
[P5814|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# class-map cmap1
Switch (config-cmap)# match access-group ip-acl
Switch (config-cmap)# quit
[P5815|Normal] 
[P5816|Item List] match-any keyword to perform a logical-OR of all matching statements under this class map. One or more match criteria must be matched. match-any any is the default mode.
[P5817|Item List] match-all = Use the match-all keyword to perform a logical-AND of all matching statements under this class map. All match criteria in the class map must be matched.
[P5818|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P5819|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5820|Heading 5] step 5 Validation
[P5821|Terminal Display] Switch# show class-map cmap1
    CLASS-MAP-NAME: cmap1 (match-any)
      match access-group: ip-acl
[P5822|Heading 4] Create Policy Map
[P5823|Normal] The following shows creating a policy map to classify, policer, and mark traffic. In this example it is creating a policy map, and attaching it to an ingress interface. In this example, the IP ACL allows traffic from network 10.1.0.0. If the matched traffic exceeds a 48000-kbps average traffic rate, it is dropped.
[P5824|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P5825|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5826|Heading 5] step 2 Create ACL and ACEs
[P5827|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip access-list ip-acl
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# quit
[P5828|Heading 5] step 3 Create class-map and match the ACL
[P5829|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# class-map type qos cmap1
Switch(config-cmap)# match access-group ip-acl
Switch(config-cmap)# quit
[P5830|Heading 5] step 4 Create policy-map and match the class-map; set the action in policy-class configure mode
[P5831|Terminal Display] switch(config)# policy-map type qos pmap1
switch(config-pmap)# class type qos cmap1
Switch(config-pmap-c)# policer color-blind cir 48000 cbs 10000 ebs 16000 violate drop
Switch(config-pmap-qos-c)# set traffic-class 5 
Switch(config-pmap-qos-c)# set color yellow 
Switch(config-pmap-c)# quit
Switch(config-pmap)# quit
[P5832|Normal] Use the “no policy-map” in global configure mode to remove the policy-map. Use the “no policer” in policy-class configure mode to remove the policer, Use the “no set” in policy-class configure mode to reset the default value for priority or color.(By default the priority is 0 and color is green.)
[P5833|Heading 5] step 5 Enter the interface configure mode and apply the policy-map
[P5834|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# service-policy type qos input pmap1
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P5835|Normal] Currently only one policy-map is supported per-direction for each interface. The “no service-policy input|output” command is used to unapply the policy map.
[P5836|Heading 5] step 6 Exit the configure mode
[P5837|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5838|Heading 5] step 7 Validation
[P5839|Terminal Display] Switch# show policy-map pmap1

  POLICY-MAP-NAME: pmap1 ( type qos)
    State: detached

    CLASS-MAP-NAME: cmap1
      match access-group: ip-acl
        set traffic-class       : 5
        set color               : yellow
        policer color-blind cir 48000 cbs 10000 ebs 16000 violate drop
[P5840|Heading 4] Create Aggregate Policer
[P5841|Normal] The following shows creating an aggregate policer to classify, police, and mark traffic. In this example it is creating an aggregate policer, and attaching it to multiple classes within a policy map. In this example, the IP ACLs allow traffic from network 10.1.0.0 and host 11.3.1.1. The traffic rate from network 10.1.0.0 and host 11.3.1.1 is policed. If the traffic exceeds a 48000-kbps average traffic rate and an 8000-byte normal burst size, it is considered out of profile, and is dropped. The policy map is attached to an ingress interface.
[P5842|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P5843|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5844|Heading 5] step 2 Create ACL and ACEs
[P5845|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip access-list ip-acl1
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# exit
Switch(config)# ip access-list ip-acl2
Switch(config-ip-acl)# permit any host 11.3.1.1 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# exit
[P5846|Heading 5] step 3 Create an aggregate-policer
[P5847|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# qos aggregate-policer transmit1 color-blind cir 48000 cbs 8000 ebs 10000 violate drop
[P5848|Normal] To delete the aggregate-policer, use the “no qos aggregate-policer” command.
[P5849|Heading 5] step 4 Create class-map and match the ACL
[P5850|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# class-map type qos cmap1
Switch(config-cmap)# match access-group ip-acl1
Switch(config-cmap)# exit
Switch(config)# class-map type qos cmap2
Switch(config-cmap)# match access-group ip-acl2
Switch(config-cmap)# exit
[P5851|Heading 5] step 5 Create policy-map and match the class-map; Apply the aggregate-policer in policy-class configure mode
[P5852|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# policy-map type qos aggflow1
Switch(config-pmap)# class type qos cmap1
Switch(config-pmap-c)# aggregate-policer transmit1
Switch(config-pmap-c)# exit
Switch(config-pmap)# class type qos cmap2
Switch(config-pmap-c)# aggregate-policer transmit1
Switch(config-pmap-c)# exit
Switch(config-pmap)# exit
[P5853|Normal] To remove the aggregate-policer, use the “no policer-aggregate” command in in policy-class configure mode.
[P5854|Heading 5] step 6 Enter the interface configure mode and apply the policy-map
[P5855|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# service-policy type qos input aggflow1
Switch(config-if)# exit
Switch(config)# exit
[P5856|Heading 5] step 7 Exit the configure mode
[P5857|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5858|Heading 5] step 8 Validation
[P5859|Terminal Display] Switch# show qos aggregate-policer
Aggreate policer: transmit1
  color blind
  CIR 48000 kbps, CBS 8000 bytes, EBS 10000 bytes
  drop violate packets 
[P5860|Heading 3] Configuration for Queue
[P5861|Heading 4] Configuring Schedule
[P5862|Normal] Packets are scheduled by SP between different classes and WDRR between queues in the same class.
[P5863|Body Text] The following example shows configuring schedule parameters for egress queues. In this example, traffic 5 and 6 belongs to class 6, which is highest priority. Traffic 2 belongs class 0, the bandwidth is 20%.
[P5864|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mod
[P5865|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5866|Heading 5] step 2 Create class-map and match the traffic-class
[P5867|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# class-map type traffic-class tc5
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# match traffic-class 5
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# exit

Switch(config)# class-map type traffic-class tc6
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# match traffic-class 6
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# exit

Switch(config)# class-map type traffic-class tc2
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# match traffic-class 2
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# exit
[P5868|Heading 5] step 3 Create policy-map and match the class-map； Set the priority in policy-class configure mode
[P5869|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# policy-map type traffic-class tc
Switch(config-pmap-tc)# class type traffic-class tc5
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# priority level 6
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# exit

Switch(config-pmap-tc)# class type traffic-class tc6
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# priority level 6
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# exit

Switch(config-pmap-tc)# class type traffic-class tc2
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# bandwidth percentage 20
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# exit
Switch(config-pmap-tc)# exit
[P5870|Heading 5] step 4 Enter the interface configure mode and apply the policy-map
[P5871|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# service-policy type traffic-class tc
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P5872|Heading 5] step 5 Exit the configure mode
[P5873|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5874|Heading 5] step 6 Validation
[P5875|Terminal Display] Switch# show qos interface eth-0-1 egress
TC Priority Bandwidth Shaping(kbps) Drop-Mode   Max-Queue-Limit(Cell)   ECN

[P5876|Heading 4] Configuring Tail Drop
[P5877|Normal] Tail drop is the default congestion-avoidance technique on every egress queue. With tail drop, packets are queued until the thresholds are exceeded. The following shows configuring tail drop threshold for different drop-precedence. Follow these steps from Privileged Exec mode.
[P5878|Body Text] In this example it is configuring tail drop threshold for traffic class 3. In this example, packet drop threshold is 2000.
[P5879|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P5880|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5881|Heading 5] step 2 Create class-map and match the traffic-class
[P5882|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# class-map type traffic-class tc3
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# match traffic-class 3
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# exit
[P5883|Heading 5] step 3 Create policy-map and match the class-map
[P5884|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# policy-map type traffic-class tc
Switch(config-pmap-tc)# class type traffic-class tc3
[P5885|Heading 5] step 4 Set the threshold for tail drop in policy-class configure mode
[P5886|Terminal Display] Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# queue-limit 2000
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# exit
Switch(config-pmap-tc)# exit
[P5887|Heading 5] step 5 Enter the interface configure mode and apply the policy-map
[P5888|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# service-policy type traffic-class tc
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P5889|Heading 5] step 6 Exit the configure mode
[P5890|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5891|Heading 5] step 7 Validation
[P5892|Terminal Display] Switch# show qos interface eth-0-1 egress
TC Priority Bandwidth Shaping(kbps) Drop-Mode   Max-Queue-Limit(Cell)   ECN
0  0        -         -             dynamic     level 10                 -
1  0        -         -             dynamic     level 10                 -
2  0        -         -             dynamic     level 10                 -
3  0        -         -             tail-drop   2000                    2000
4  0        -         -             dynamic     level 10                 -
5  0        -         -             dynamic     level 10                 -
6  0        -         -             dynamic     level 10                 -
7  7        -         -             tail-drop   64                      -
[P5893|Heading 4] Configuring WRED
[P5894|Normal] WRED reduces the chances of tail drop by selectively dropping packets when the output interface detects congestion. By dropping some packets early rather than waiting until the queue is full, WRED avoids TCP synchronization dropping and thereafter improves the overall network throughput.
[P5895|Body Text] The following example shows configuring WRED threshold for traffic class 1. In this example, the max-threshold is 596, min-threshold is 596/8=71. If buffered packets exceed min-threshold, the subsequent packet will be dropped randomly.
[P5896|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P5897|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P5898|Heading 5] step 2 Create class-map and match the traffic-class
[P5899|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# class-map type traffic-class tc1
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# match traffic-class 1
Switch(config-cmap-tc)# exit
[P5900|Heading 5] step 3 Create policy-map and match the class-map
[P5901|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# policy-map type traffic-class tc
Switch(config-pmap-tc)# class type traffic-class tc1
[P5902|Heading 5] step 4 Set the threshold for WRED in policy-class configure mode
[P5903|Terminal Display] Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# random-detect maximum-threshold 596
Switch(config-pmap-tc-c)# exit
Switch(config-pmap-tc)# exit
[P5904|Heading 5] step 5 Enter the interface configure mode and apply the policy-map
[P5905|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# service-policy type traffic-class tc
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P5906|Heading 5] step 6 Exit the configure mode
[P5907|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P5908|Heading 5] step 7 Validation

[P5929|Heading 4] Configuring Port policing
[P5930|Normal] All traffic received or transmitted in the physical interface can be limited rate, and all the exceeding traffic will be dropped.
[P5931|Body Text] The following example shows creating an ingress port policer. In this example, if the received traffic exceeds a 48000-kbps average traffic rate, it is dropped.

Switch(config-if)# qos policer input color-blind cir 48000 cbs 10000 ebs 20000 violate drop
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P5936|Normal]  To remove the configuration of policer, use the “no port-policier input|output” command.

[P5989|Heading 1] IPv6 Service Configuration
[P5990|Heading 2] Configuring IPv6 over IPv4 Tunnel
[P5991|Heading 3] Overview
[P5992|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P5993|Normal] Tunneling is an encapsulation technology, which uses one network protocol to encapsulate packets of another network protocol and transfer them over a virtual point-to-point connection. The virtual connection is called a tunnel. Tunneling refers to the whole process from data encapsulation to data transfer and data decapsulation.
[P5994|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P5995|Normal] 
[P5996|Figure Description] IPv6 over IPv4 Tunnel
[P5997|Body Text] Overlay tunneling encapsulates IPv6 packets in IPv4 packets for delivery across an IPv4 infrastructure (a core network or the Internet. By using overlay tunnels, you can communicate with isolated IPv6 networks without upgrading the IPv4 infrastructure between them. Overlay tunnels can be configured between border routers or between a border router and a host; however, both tunnel endpoints must support both the IPv4 and IPv6 protocol stacks. The IPv6 over IPv4 tunnel processes packets in the following ways:
[P5998|Item List] A host in the IPv6 network sends an IPv6 packet to Switch1 at the tunnel source.
[P5999|Item List] After determining according to the routing table that the packet needs to be forwarded through the tunnel, Switch1 encapsulates the IPv6 packet with an IPv4 header and forwards it through the physical interface of the tunnel.
[P6000|Item List] Upon receiving the packet, Switch2 decapsulates the packet.
[P6001|Item List] Switch2 forwards the packet according to the destination address in the de-encapsulated IPv6 packet. If the destination address is the device itself, Switch2 forwards the IPv6 packet to the upper-layer protocol for processing.
[P6002|Normal] The benefit of the technique is that current ipv4 networks do not need to update on all nodes. Only the edge nodes are required to support dual stack and tunnel.
[P6003|Body Text] IPv6 over IPv4 tunnels are divided into manually configured tunnels and automatic tunnels, depending on how the IPv4 address of the tunnel destination is acquired:
[P6004|Item List] Manually configured tunnel: The destination address of the tunnel cannot be automatically acquired through the destination IPv6 address of an IPv6 packet at the tunnel source, and must be manually configured.
[P6005|Item List] Automatic tunnel: The destination address of the tunnel is an IPv6 address with an IPv4 address embedded, and the IPv4 address can be automatically acquired through the destination IPv6 address of an IPv6 packet at the tunnel source.
[P6006|Normal] Normally, system supports the following types of overlay tunneling mechanisms:
[P6007|Item List] Manual
[P6008|Item List] 6to4
[P6009|Item List] Intra-site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP)
[P6010|Normal] The details of the 3 types of overlay tunneling mechanisms are described below：
[P6011|Heading 5] Manual Tunnel
[P6012|Normal] A manually configured tunnel is equivalent to a permanent link between two IPv6 domains over an IPv4 backbone. The primary use is for stable connections that require regular secure communication between two edge routers or between an end system and an edge router, or for connection to remote IPv6 networks.
[P6013|Body Text] An IPv6 address is manually configured on a tunnel interface, and manually configured IPv4 addresses are assigned to the tunnel source and the tunnel destination. The host or router at each end of a configured tunnel must support both the IPv4 and IPv6 protocol stacks. Manually configured tunnels can be configured between border routers or between a border router and a host.
[P6014|Heading 5] 6to4 Tunnel
[P6015|Normal] Ordinary 6to4 tunnel
[P6016|Item List] An automatic 6to4 tunnel allows isolated IPv6 domains to be connected over an IPv4 network to remote IPv6 networks. The key difference between automatic 6to4 tunnels and manually configured tunnels is that the tunnel is not point-to-point; it is point-to-multipoint. In automatic 6to4 tunnels, routers are not configured in pairs because they treat the IPv4 infrastructure as a virtual non-broadcast multi-access (NBMA) link. The IPv4 address embedded in the IPv6 address is used to find the other end of the automatic tunnel.
[P6017|Item List] An automatic 6to4 tunnel may be configured on a border router in an isolated IPv6 network, which creates a tunnel on a per-packet basis to a border router in another IPv6 network over an IPv4 infrastructure. The tunnel destination is determined by the IPv4 address of the border router extracted from the IPv6 address that starts with the prefix 2002::/16, where the format is 2002:border-router-IPv4-address::/48.
[P6018|Item List] Following the embedded IPv4 address are 16 bits that can be used to number networks within the site. The border router at each end of a 6to4 tunnel must support both the IPv4 and IPv6 protocol stacks. 6to4 tunnels are configured between border routers or between a border router and a host.
[P6019|Normal] 6to4 relay
[P6020|Body Text] A 6to4 tunnel is only used to connect 6to4 networks, whose IP prefix must be 2002::/16. However, IPv6 network addresses with the prefix such as 2001::/16 may also be used in IPv6 networks. To connect a 6to4 network to an IPv6 network, a 6to4 router must be used as a gateway to forward packets to the IPv6 network. Such a router is called 6to4 relay router.
[P6021|Normal] 
[P6022|Figure Description] IPv6 over IPv4 Tunnel
[P6023|Body Text] As shown in the above figure, a static route must be configured on the border router (Switch1) in the 6to4 network and the next-hop address must be the 6to4 address of the 6to4 relay router (Switch3). In this way, all packets destined for the IPv6 network will be forwarded to the 6to4 relay router, and then to the IPv6 network. Thus, interworking between the 6to4 network (with the address prefix starting with 2002) and the IPv6 network is realized.
[P6024|Heading 5] ISATAP Tunnel
[P6025|Normal] ISATAP is an automatic overlay tunneling mechanism that uses the underlying IPv4 network as a NBMA link layer for IPv6. ISATAP is designed for transporting IPv6 packets within a site where a native IPv6 infrastructure is not yet available; for example, when sparse IPv6 hosts are deployed for testing. ISATAP tunnels allow individual IPv4 or IPv6 dual-stack hosts within a site to communicate with other such hosts on the same virtual link, basically creating an IPv6 network using the IPv4 infrastructure.
[P6026|Body Text] When an ISATAP tunnel is used, the destination address of an IPv6 packet and the IPv6 address of a tunnel interface both adopt special ISATAP addresses. ISATAP uses a well-defined IPv6 address format composed of any unicast IPv6 prefix (/64), which can be link local, or global (including 6to4 prefixes), enabling IPv6 routing locally or on the Internet. The IPv4 address is encoded in the last 32 bits of the IPv6 address, enabling automatic IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling. The ISATAP address format is prefix(64bit):0:5EFE: IPv4-address.
[P6027|Normal] 
[P6028|Figure Description] ISATAP Tunnel
[P6029|Body Text] The ISATAP router provides standard router advertisement network configuration support for the ISATAP site. This feature allows clients to automatically configure themselves as they would do if they were connected to an Ethernet. It can also be configured to provide connectivity out of the site.
[P6030|Body Text] Although the ISATAP tunneling mechanism is similar to other automatic tunneling mechanisms, such as IPv6 6to4 tunneling, ISATAP is designed for transporting IPv6 packets within a site, not between sites.
[P6031|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6032|Heading 4] Configure Manual Tunnel
[P6033|Normal] 
[P6034|Figure Description] Manual Tunnel
[P6035|Body Text] As shown in the above Figure, two IPv6 networks are connected over an IPv4 network. Configure an IPv6 manual tunnel between Switch1 and Switch2 to make the two IPv6 networks reachable to each other.
[P6036|Body Text] 
[P6037|Item List] Must enable IPv6/IPv4 dual stack before tunnel configuration.
[P6038|Item List] Make sure tunnel destination is reachable in the IPv4 network.
[P6039|Item List] There must exist an IPv6 address in the tunnel interface, otherwise routes with tunnel interface as nexthop will be invalid.
[P6040|Normal] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P6041|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6042|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6043|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 globally
[P6044|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable
[P6045|Heading 5] step 3 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P6046|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch1:
[P6047|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1/24
Switch(config-if)# tunnel enable
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 3002::1/64
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface tunnel1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel source eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel destination 192.168.20.1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel mode ipv6ip
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 3001::1/64
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6048|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch2:
[P6049|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport

Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport

Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface tunnel1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel source eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel destination 192.168.10.1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel mode ipv6ip
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 3001::2/64
Switch(config-if)# exit

[P6067|Heading 4] Configure 6to4 Tunnel
[P6068|Normal] 
[P6069|Figure Description] 6to4 tunnel
[P6070|Body Text] As shown in the above Figure, two 6to4 networks are connected to an IPv4 network through two 6to4 routers (Switch1 and Switch2) respectively. Configure a 6to4 tunnel to make Host1 and Host2 reachable to each other.
[P6071|Body Text] To enable communication between 6to4 networks, you need to configure 6to4 addresses for 6to4 routers and hosts in the 6to4 networks.
[P6072|Body Text] The IPv4 address of eth-0-1 on Switch1 is 2.1.1.1/24, and the corresponding 6to4 prefix is 2002:0201:0101::/48 after it is translated to an IPv6 address. Assign interface tunnel 1 to subnet 2002:0201:0101::/64 and eth-0-2 to subnet 2002:0201:0101:1::/64.
[P6073|Body Text] The IPv4 address of eth-0-1 on Switch2 is 5.1.1.1/24, and the corresponding 6to4 prefix is 2002:0501:0101::/48 after it is translated to an IPv6 address. Assign interface tunnel 1 to subnet 2002:0501:0101::/64 and eth-0-2 to subnet 2002:0501:0101:1::/64.
[P6074|Body Text] 
[P6075|Item List] No destination address needs to be configured for a 6to4 tunnel
[P6076|Item List] The automatic tunnel interfaces using the same encapsulation protocol cannot share the same source IP address
[P6077|Item List] To encapsulate and forward IPv6 packets whose destination address does not belong to the network segment where the receiving tunnel interface resides, you need to configure a static route to reach the destination IPv6 address through this tunnel interface on the router. Because automatic tunnels do not support dynamic routing, you can configure a static route to that destination IPv6 address with this tunnel interface as the outbound interface or the peer tunnel interface address as the next hop
[P6078|Item List] Only on4 6to4 tunnel can exist in the same node.
[P6079|Normal] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P6080|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6081|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6082|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 globally
[P6083|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable
[P6084|Heading 5] step 3 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P6085|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch1:
[P6086|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ip address 2.1.1.1/24
Switch(config-if)# tunnel enable
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 2002:201:101:1::1/64
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface tunnel1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel source eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel mode ipv6ip 6to4
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 2002:201:101::1/64
Switch(config-if)# exit

[P6108|Figure Description] 6to4 relay
[P6109|Body Text] As shown in the above Figure, Switch1 is a 6to4 router, and 6to4 addresses are used on the connected IPv6 network. Switch2 serves as a 6to4 relay router and is connected to the IPv6 network (2001::/16). Configure a 6to4 tunnel between Router A and Router B to make Host A and Host B reachable to each other.
[P6110|Body Text] 
[P6111|Item List] The configuration on a 6to4 relay router is similar to that on a 6to4 router. However, to enable communication between the 6to4 network and the IPv6 network, you need to configure a route to the IPv6 network on the 6to4 router.
[P6112|Item List] It is not allowed to change the tunnel mode from 6to4 to ISATAP when there are any 6to4 relay routes existing. You must delete this route first.

[P6140|Heading 4] Configure ISATAP Tunnel
[P6141|Normal] 
[P6142|Figure Description] ISATAP tunnel
[P6143|Body Text] As shown in the above Figure, an IPv6 network is connected to an IPv4 network through an ISATAP router. It is required that the IPv6 host in the IPv4 network can access the IPv6 network through the ISATAP tunnel.
[P6144|Body Text] 
[P6145|Item List] No destination address needs to be configured for a ISATAP tunnel
[P6146|Item List] The automatic tunnel interfaces using the same encapsulation protocol cannot share the same source IP address
[P6147|Item List] To encapsulate and forward IPv6 packets whose destination address does not belong to the network segment where the receiving tunnel interface resides, you need to configure a static route to reach the destination IPv6 address through this tunnel interface on the router. Because automatic tunnels do not support dynamic routing, you can configure a static route to that destination IPv6 address with this tunnel interface as the outbound interface or the peer tunnel interface address as the next hop
[P6148|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6149|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6150|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 globally
[P6151|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable
[P6152|Heading 5] step 3 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P6153|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ip address 1.1.1.1/24
Switch(config-if)# tunnel enable
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 3001::1/64
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface tunnel1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel source eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel mode ipv6ip isatap
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001::/64 eui-64
Switch(config-if)# no ipv6 nd ra suppress

Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6154|Heading 5] step 4 Create static routes
[P6155|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip route 2.1.1.0/24 1.1.1.2
Switch(config)# ipv6 route 2001::/16 tunnel1

[P6157|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# arp 1.1.1.2 0.0.2222

[P6174|Heading 2] Configuring ND
[P6175|Heading 3] Overview
[P6176|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6177|Normal] Nodes (hosts and routers) use Neighbor Discovery to determine the link-layer addresses for neighbors known to reside on attached links and to quickly purge cached values that become invalid.
[P6178|Body Text] Hosts also use Neighbor Discovery to find neighboring routers that are willing to forward packets on their behalf.
[P6179|Body Text] Finally, nodes use the protocol to actively keep track of which neighbors are reachable and which are not, and to detect changed link-layer addresses. When a router or the path to a router fails, a host actively searches for functioning alternates.
[P6180|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6181|Normal] N/A
[P6182|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6183|Normal] 
[P6184|Figure Description] NDP
[P6185|Body Text] In this example, interface eth-0-1 assigned with ipv6 address 3000::1/64, on subnet 3000::/64, there are two hosts, and their IP addresses are 3000::2, 3000::3, MAC address are 001a-a011-eca2, 001a-a011-eca3. Neighbor entry of host 3000::2 is added manually, the entry of host 3000::3 is added dynamically. The reachable time of neighbor entries for interface eth-0-1 configure to 10 minutes, NS interval on interface eth-0-1 configure to 2 seconds.
[P6186|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6187|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6188|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P6189|Terminal Display] Switch (config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch (config-if)# no switchport
Switch (config-if)# no shutdown
Switch (config-if)# ipv6 address 3000::1/64
Switch (config-if)# ipv6 nd reachable-time 600
Switch (config-if)# ipv6 nd ns-interval 2000
Switch (config-if)# exit
[P6190|Heading 5] step 3 Add a static neighbor entry
[P6191|Terminal Display] Switch (config)# ipv6 neighbor 3000::2 001a.a011.eca2
[P6192|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P6193|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P6194|Heading 5] step 5 Validation
[P6195|Terminal Display] Switch # show ipv6 neighbors

3000::3                                  6        001a-a011-eca3  REACH eth-0-1
fe80::6d8:e8ff:fe4c:e700                 6        001a-a011-eca3  STALE eth-0-1
[P6196|Heading 2] Configuring DHCPv6 Relay
[P6197|Heading 3] Overview
[P6198|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6199|Normal] DHCPv6 relay is any host that forwards DHCPv6 packets between clients and servers. Relay is used to forward requests and replies between clients and servers when they are not on the same physical subnet. Relay forwarding is distinct from the normal forwarding of an IPv6 router, where IPv6 datagram are switched between networks somewhat transparently.
[P6200|Body Text] By contrast, relay receive DHCPv6 messages and then generate a new DHCPv6 message to send out on another interface. The relay sets the link address (used by server to identify the subnet that client is belong to), and, if configured, adds the remote-id option in the packet and forwards it to the DHCPv6 server..
[P6201|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6202|Normal] N/A
[P6203|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6204|Normal] 
[P6205|Figure Description] DHCP Relay
[P6206|Body Text] This figure is the networking topology for testing DHCPv6 relay functions. We need two Linux boxes and one Switch to construct the test bed.
[P6207|Item List] Computer A is used as DHCPv6 server.
[P6208|Item List] Computer B is used as DHCPv6 client.
[P6209|Item List] Switch is used as DHCPv6 relay.
[P6210|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6211|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6212|Heading 5] step 2 Enable DHCPv6 relay globally
[P6213|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# service dhcpv6 enable
Switch(config)# dhcpv6 relay
Switch(config)# dhcpv6 relay remote-id option
Switch(config)# dhcpv6 relay pd route
[P6214|Heading 5] step 3 Configure the DHCPv6 server
[P6215|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# dhcpv6-server 1 2001:1000::1
[P6216|Heading 5] step 4 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P6217|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-12
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:1000::2/64
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-11
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:1001::1/64
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# dhcpv6-server 1
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6218|Heading 5] step 5 Exit the configure mode
[P6219|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end

[P6233|Heading 1] IPv6 Security Configuration Guide
[P6234|Heading 2] DHCPv6 Snooping Configuration
[P6235|Heading 3] Overview
[P6236|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6237|Normal] DHCPv6 snooping is a security feature that acts like a firewall between untrusted hosts and trusted DHCPv6 servers. The DHCPv6 snooping feature performs the following activities:
[P6238|Item List] Validate DHCPv6 messages received from untrusted sources and filters out invalid messages.
[P6239|Item List] Build and maintain the DHCPv6 snooping binding database, which contains information about untrusted hosts with leased IPv6 addresses.
[P6240|Item List] The DHCPv6 snooping feature is implemented in software basis. All DHCPv6 messages are intercepted in the chip and directed to the CPU for processing.
[P6241|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6242|Normal] N/A
[P6243|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6244|Normal] 
[P6245|Figure Description] DHCPv6 Snooping
[P6246|Body Text] This figure is the networking topology for testing DHCPv6 snooping functions. We need two PCs and one switch to construct the test bed.
[P6247|Item List] PC A is used as a DHCPv6 server.
[P6248|Item List] PC B is used as a DHCPv6 client.
[P6249|Item List] Switch A is used as a DHCPv6 Snooping device.

Switch(config-vlan)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-12
Switch(config-if)# switchport

Switch(config-if)# dhcpv6 snooping trust
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

[P6271|Heading 1] IPv6 Routing Configuration
[P6272|Heading 2] Configuring IPv6 Unicast-Routing
[P6273|Heading 3] Overview
[P6274|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6275|Normal] Static routing is a concept describing one way of configuring path selection of routers in computer networks. It is the type of routing characterized by the absence of communication between routers regarding the current topology of the network. This is achieved by manually adding routes to the routing table. The opposite of static routing is dynamic routing, sometimes also referred to as adaptive routing.
[P6276|Body Text] In these systems, routes through a data network are described by fixed paths (statically). These routes are usually entered into the router by the system administrator. An entire network can be configured using static routes, but this type of configuration is not fault tolerant. When there is a change in the network or a failure occurs between two statically defined nodes, traffic will not be rerouted. This means that anything that wishes to take an affected path will either have to wait for the failure to be repaired or the static route to be updated by the administrator before restarting its journey. Most requests will time out (ultimately failing) before these repairs can be made. There are, however, times when static routes can improve the performance of a network. Some of these include stub networks and default routes.
[P6277|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6278|Normal] N/A
[P6279|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6280|Normal] 
[P6281|Figure Description] ipv6 unicast routing

Switch(config-if)# exit

[P6313|Heading 2] Configuring OSPFv3
[P6314|Heading 3] Overview
[P6315|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6316|Normal] OSPF is an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) designed expressly for IP networks, supporting IP subnet ting and tagging of externally derived routing information.
[P6317|Body Text] The implementation conforms to the OSPF Version 3, which is described in RFC 5340, expands on OSPF version 2 to support IPv6 routing prefixes. Much of the OSPF for IPv6 feature is the same as in OSPF version 2. Changes between OSPF for IPv4, OSPF Version 2, and OSPF for IPv6 as described herein include the following:
[P6318|Item List] Addressing semantics have been removed from OSPFv3 packets and the basic Link State Advertisements (LSAs).
[P6319|Item List] OSPFv3 now runs on a per-link basis rather than on a per-IP-subnet basis.
[P6320|Item List] Authentication has been removed from the OSPFv3 protocol.
[P6321|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6322|Normal] The OSPFv3 module is based on the following RFC: RFC 5340 – OSPF for IPv6
[P6323|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6324|Heading 4] Basic OSPFv3 Parameters Configuration
[P6325|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode

Switch(config-router)# exit

[P6392|Heading 4] Configuring OSPFv3 Area Parameters
[P6393|Normal] 
[P6394|Figure Description] OSPFv3 area
[P6395|Body Text] You can optionally configure several OSPFv3 area parameters. These parameters include authentication for password-based protection against unauthorized access to an area and stub areas. Stub areas are areas into which information on external routes is not sent. Instead, the area border router (ABR) generates a default external route into the stub area for destinations outside the autonomous system (AS).
[P6396|Body Text] Route summarization is the consolidation of advertised addresses into a single summary route to be advertised by other areas. If network numbers are contiguous, you can use the area range router configuration command to configure the ABR to advertise a summary route that covers all networks in the range.
[P6397|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P6398|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6399|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6400|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 globally
[P6401|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable
[P6402|Heading 5] step 3 Create OSPFv3 instance
[P6403|Normal] Configuring Switch1:
[P6404|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# router ipv6 ospf 100 
Switch(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1

[P6431|Heading 4] Redistributing Routes into OSPFv3
[P6432|Normal] 
[P6433|Figure Description] OSPFv3 Redistribute
[P6434|Body Text] In this example the configuration causes RIPng routes to be imported into the OSPFv3 routing table and advertised as Type 5 External LSAs into Area 0.
[P6435|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P6436|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6437|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6438|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 globally
[P6439|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable
[P6440|Heading 5] step 3 Create OSPFv3 instance
[P6441|Normal] Configuring Switch1:
[P6442|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# router ipv6 ospf 100 
Switch(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
Switch(config-router)# exit
[P6443|Normal] Configuring Switch2:
[P6444|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# router ipv6 ospf 200 
Switch(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
Switch(config-router)# exit
[P6445|Normal] Configuring Switch3:
[P6446|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# router ipv6 ospf 300 
Switch(config-router)# router-id 3.3.3.3
Switch(config-router)# redistribute ripng
Switch(config-router)# exit

Switch(config-router)# exit

[P6472|Heading 4] Configure OSPFv3 Cost
[P6473|Normal] 
[P6474|Figure Description] OSPFv3 Cost
[P6475|Body Text] You can make a route the preferred route by changing its cost. In this example, cost has been configured to make Switch2 the next hop for Switch1.
[P6476|Body Text] The default cost on each interface is 1(1000M speed). Interface eth2 on Switch2 has a cost of 100 and interface eth2 on Switch3 has a cost of 150. The total cost to reach(Switch4 network 10.10.14.0) through Switch2 and Switch3:
[P6477|Body Text] Switch2: 1+1+100 = 102 Switch3: 1+1+150 = 152
[P6478|Body Text] Therefore, Switch1 chooses Switch2 as its next hop for destination Switch4
[P6479|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6480|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6481|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 globally
[P6482|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable

[P6522|Heading 3] Application cases
[P6523|Normal] N/A
[P6524|Heading 2] Configuring RIPng
[P6525|Heading 3] Overview
[P6526|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6527|Normal] Routing Information Protocol Next Generation (RIPng) is an IPv6 route exchange protocol that uses a distance vector (a number representing distance) to measure the cost of a given route. The cost is a distance vector because the cost is often equivalent to the number of router hops between the source and the destination networks. RIPng can receive multiple paths to a destination. The system evaluates the paths, selects the best path, and saves the path in the IPv6 route table as the route to the destination.
[P6528|Body Text] Typically, the best path is the path with the fewest hops. A hop is another router through which packets must travel to reach the destination. If RIPng receives a RIPng update from another router that contains a path with fewer hops than the path stored in the route table, the system replaces the older route with the newer one. The system then includes the new path in the updates it sends to other RIPng routers. RIPng routers also can modify a route’s cost, generally by adding to it, to bias the selection of a route for a given destination. In this case, the actual number of router hops may be the same, but the route has an administratively higher cost and is thus less likely to be used than other, lower-cost routes. A RIPng route can have a maximum cost of 15. Any destination with a higher cost is considered unreachable. Although limiting to larger networks, the low maximum hop count prevents endless loops in the network.
[P6529|Body Text] This chapter contains basic RIPng configuration examples. To see details on the commands used in these examples, or to see the outputs of the Validation commands, refer to the RIPng Command Reference. To avoid repetition, some Common commands, like configure terminal, have not been listed under the Commands Used section.
[P6530|Body Text] There are some differences between RIPng and RIP:
[P6531|Item List] UDP port number: RIPng uses UDP port number 521 to send or receive package.
[P6532|Item List] Multicast address: RIPng uses FF02::9 to multicast package to other routers of link local.
[P6533|Item List] Nexthop address: RIPng uses 128 bit ipv6 address.
[P6534|Item List] Source address: RIPng uses IPv6 link-local address FE80::/10 to be the source address when updating package to neighbor.
[P6535|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6536|Normal] The RIPng module is based on the following RFC: RFC 2080 – RIPng for IPv6
[P6537|Heading 3] Configuration

[P6559|Heading 4] Configuring Metric Parameters
[P6560|Normal] A RIPng offset list allows you to add to the metric of specific inbound or outbound routes learned or advertised by RIPng. RIPng offset lists provide a simple method for adding to the cost of specific routes and therefore biasing the router’s route selection away from those routes. An offset list consists of the following parameters:
[P6561|Item List] An ACL that specifies the routes to which to add the metric.
[P6562|Item List] In: applies to routes the router learns from RIPng neighbors.
[P6563|Item List] Out: applies to routes the router is advertising to its RIPng neighbors.
[P6564|Item List] The offset value that will be added to the routing metric of the routes that match the ACL.
[P6565|Item List] The interface that the offset list applies (optional).
[P6566|Normal] If a route matches both a global offset list (without specified interface) and an interface-based offset list, the interface-based offset list takes precedence. The interface-based offset list’s metric is added to the route in this case.
[P6567|Normal] 
[P6568|Figure Description] RIPng Metric

[P6589|Heading 4] Configuring the Administrative Distance
[P6590|Normal] By default, RIPng assigns the default RIPng administrative distance (120) to RIPng routes. When comparing routes based on administrative distance, the router selects the route with the lower distance. You can change the administrative distance for RIPng routes.

[P6611|Heading 4] Configuring Redistribution
[P6612|Normal] You can configure the router to redistribute static routes, direct connected routes or routes learned through Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) into RIPng. When you redistribute a route from one of these other protocols into RIPng, the router can use RIPng to advertise the route to its RIPng neighbors.
[P6613|Body Text] Change the default redistribution metric (optional). The router assigns a RIPng metric of 1 to each redistributed route by default. You can change the default metric to a value up to 16.
[P6614|Body Text] Enable specified routes to redistribute with default or specified metric.
[P6615|Normal]

[P6639|Heading 4] Configuring Split-horizon Parameters
[P6640|Normal] Normally, routers that are connected to multicast-type IPv6 networks and that use distance-vector routing protocols employ the split horizon mechanism to reduce the possibility of routing loops. Split horizon blocks information about routes from being advertised by a router out of any interface from which that information originated. This behavior usually optimizes communications among multiple routers, particularly when links are broken. However, with non-multicast networks (such as Frame Relay), situations can arise for which this behavior is less than ideal. For these situations, you might want to disable split horizon for RIPng.
[P6641|Body Text] You can avoid including routes in updates sent to the same gateway from which they were learned. Using the split horizon command omits routes learned from one neighbor, in updates sent to that neighbor. Using the poisoned parameter with this command includes such routes in updates, but sets their metrics to infinity. Thus, advertising these routes means that they are not reachable.
[P6642|Normal] 
[P6643|Figure Description] RIPng Split-horizon

[P6667|Heading 4] Configuring Timers
[P6668|Normal] RIPng use several timers that determine such variables as the frequency of routing updates, the length of time before a route becomes invalid, and other parameters. You can adjust these timers to tune RIPng performance to better suit your internet-work needs. You can make the following timer adjustments:
[P6669|Item List] The rate (time in seconds between updates) at which routing updates are sent.
[P6670|Item List] The interval of time (in seconds) after which a route is declared invalid.
[P6671|Item List] The amount of time (in seconds) that must pass before a route is removed from the routing table.
[P6672|Normal] To configure the timers, use the following command:
[P6673|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6674|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6675|Heading 5] step 2 Set the timers
[P6676|Normal] Set the routing table update timer to 10 seconds. Set the routing information timeout timer to 180 seconds. Set the routing garbage collection timer to 120 seconds.
[P6677|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# router ipv6 rip
Switch(config-router)# timers basic 10 180 120
Switch(config-router)# exit
[P6678|Heading 5] step 3 Exit the configure mode
[P6679|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P6680|Heading 5] step 4 Validation
[P6681|Normal] Use the commands as follows to validate the configuration:

[P6683|Heading 4] Configuring RIPng Route Distribute Filters
[P6684|Normal] A RIP distribute list allows you to permit or deny learning or advertising of specific routes. A distribute list consists of the following parameters:
[P6685|Item List] An ACL or a prefix list that filter the routes.
[P6686|Item List] In: filter applies to learned routes.
[P6687|Item List] Out: filter applies to advertised routes
[P6688|Item List] The interface that the filer applies (optional).
[P6689|Normal]

[P6712|Heading 2] Configuring Ipv6 Prefix-list
[P6713|Heading 3] Overview
[P6714|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6715|Normal] Routing Policy is the technology for modifying route information to change traffic route. IPv6 Prefix list is a kind of route policies that used to control and modify routing information. A IPv6 prefix list is identified by list name and contains one or more ordered entries which are processed sequentially. Each entry provides a matched range for network prefix and has a unique sequence number in the list. In the matching process，switch will check entries orderly. If an entry matches conditions, this process would finish.
[P6716|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6717|Normal] N/A
