[P6754|Heading 2] ConfiguringIPv6 PBR
[P6755|Heading 3] Overview
[P6756|Heading 4] Brief Introduction
[P6757|Normal] Different from forwarding ipv6 packets based on destination address, PBR is a mechanism that forwards routes based on user-defined policies. Packets that meet certain conditions will be forwared according to the specified behavior. Users can set different next-hop based on different packet characteristics to implement flexible routing and forwarding.
[P6758|Heading 5] Process of Forwarding IPv6 Packets
[P6759|Normal] After packets arrive, system will perform the forwarding operation in the following sequence:
[P6760|Item List] Match the route-map. If any route-map configured next-hop is matched, packets will be forwarded according to this matched next-hop.

[P6761|Item List] If no next-hop of route-map is matched, packets will be forwarded according to specific route.

[P6762|Item List] If there is no specfic route, but any route-map configured default next-hop is matched, packets will be forwared according to this matched default next-hop.

[P6763|Item List] If the preceding conditions are not met, packets will be forwared according to the default-route.
[P6764|Normal] The prioritties of packet forwarding can be considered as follows:
PBR next-hop > Specific Route > PBR default next-hop > Default Route
[P6765|Heading 5] ACL and route-map in IPv6 PBR
[P6766|Item List] Matching rules for IPv6 PBR:
[P6767|Item List] In IPv6 PBR, access control list (ACL) are used to match packets, and ACL clauses include two types: permit and deny.
[P6768|Item List] The matching features supported by IPv6 PBR include IPv6 source address, IPv6 destination address, protocol type, and port number.
[P6769|Item List] Currently, IPv6 PBR only supports permit type ACL clauses and ignores deny type clauses.
[P6770|Item List] Routing policies for IPv6 PBR:
[P6771|Item List] In IPv6 PBR, route-map are used to determine the combination of ACL used to match packets and the forwarding next hop after matching.
[P6772|Item List] By setting match rules and set rules to specify the forwarding behavior of PBR, IPv6 PBR match rule is “match ipv6 address,” set rules are “set ipv6 nexthop” or “set ipv6 default nexthop.”
[P6773|Item List] Route-map consist of permit and deny sequences, with IPv6 PBR only supporting permit type route-map sequences and ignoring deny type sequences.
[P6774|Item List] Relationship between packet matching results and types of ACL and route-map sequences:
[P6775|Item List] If there are multiple permit clauses in an ACL, the ACL matching result is a hit as long as it matches one of the permit clauses; if none of the permit clauses can match the packet, the matching result is a miss.
[P6776|Item List] If the ACL matching result is a hit, the corresponding route-map sequence is also a hit, and the packet will be forwarded according to the set rules of that sequence.
[P6777|Item List] Route-map sequences have priorities, with higher priority sequences matched first; if a match is found, the packet is directly forwarded. If no match is found, the sequences are progressively matched by priority until a sequence is hit, or there are no more sequences to match.
[P6778|Heading 3] Configuration Examples
[P6779|Heading 4] IPv6 PBR Configuration
[P6780|Heading 5] Topology
[P6781|Normal] 
[P6782|Figure Description] Typical networking diagram of IPv6 PBR
[P6783|Body Text] The figure above is a typical topology: After Enabling PBR on interface eth-0-1 of Switch1, packets from 3000::1 should be forwarded to 3020::2, and other packets should be forwarded according to the original routes.
[P6784|Body Text] Configure on Switch1:
[P6785|Heading 5] Configuration Steps
[P6786|Step] Enter the configure mode
[P6787|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6788|Step] Create an IPv6 access list to match source ip address
[P6789|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 access-list acl1
Switch(config-ip-acl)# 10 permit any 3000::1/128 any
Switch(config-ip-acl)# exit
[P6790|Step] Create a route map, to match the IPv6 access list and set the nexthop ip
[P6791|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# route-map rmap permit 10
Switch(config-route-map)# match ipv6 address acl1
Switch(config-route-map)# set ipv6 next-hop 3020::2
Switch(config-route-map)# exit
[P6792|Step] Enter the interface configure mode, set the attributes and ip address, and apply the route map
[P6793|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 3020::1/64
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# ip policy route-map rmap
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6794|Step] Create a static route with the nexthop ip 3020::3 (optional)
[P6795|Body Text] To forwarding the packets which not hit the PBR, we can use a static route. Dynamic protocols such as RIP/OSPF are can also meet this requirement.
[P6796|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 route 0::0/0 3020::3
[P6797|Step] Exit the configure mode
[P6798|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P6799|Step] Validation
[P6800|Normal] Switch# show ip policy route-map
Route-map                     interface 
rmap                          eth-0-1
[P6801|Heading 1] IPv6 Multicast Configuration Guide
[P6802|Heading 2] Configuring IPv6 Multicast-Routing
[P6803|Heading 3] Overview
[P6804|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6805|Normal] Multicast protocols allow a group or channel to be accessed over different networks by multiple stations (clients) for the receipt and transmit of multicast data.
[P6806|Body Text] Distribution of stock quotes, video transmissions such as news services and remote classrooms, and video conferencing are all examples of applications that use multicast routing.
[P6807|Item List] Mulitcast Listener Discovery (MLD) is used among hosts on a LAN and the routers (and multilayer switches) on that LAN to track the multicast groups of which hosts are members.
[P6808|Item List] Protocol-Independent Multicast (PIM) protocol is used among routers and multilayer switches to track which multicast packets to forward to each other and to their directly connected LANs. PIM has two modes: Sparse-mode and Dense-mode. Currently, we only support Sparse-mode
[P6809|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6810|Normal] N/A
[P6811|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6812|Heading 4] Configuring IPv6 multicast route limit
[P6813|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6814|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6815|Heading 5] step 2 Set the limit of the IPv6 multicast route
[P6816|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 multicast route-limit 1000
[P6817|Heading 5] step 3 Exit the configure mode
[P6818|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P6819|Heading 5] step 4 Validation
[P6820|Terminal Display] Switch# show ipv6 mroute route-limit 
IPv6 Max Multicast Route Limit Number: 1000
IPv6 Multicast Route Limit Warning Threshold: 1000
IPv6 Multicast Hardware Route Limit: 255
IPv6 Current Multicast Route Entry Number: 0
[P6821|Heading 3] Application cases
[P6822|Normal] N/A
[P6823|Heading 2] Configuring MLD
[P6824|Heading 3] Overview
[P6825|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6826|Normal] To participate in IPv6 multicasting, multicast hosts, routers, and multilayer switches must have the MLD operating. This protocol defines the query and host roles:
[P6827|Item List] A query is a network device that sends query messages to discover which network devices are members of a given multicast group.
[P6828|Item List] A host is a receiver that sends report messages (in response to query messages) to inform a querier of a host membership.
[P6829|Item List] A set of queries and hosts that receive IPv6 multicast data streams from the same source is called an IPv6 multicast group. Queries and hosts use MLD messages to join and leave IPv6 multicast groups. Any host, regardless of whether it is a member of a group, can send to a group. However, only the members of a group receive the message. Membership in a multicast group is dynamic; hosts can join and leave at any time. There is no restriction on the location or number of members in a multicast group.
[P6830|Item List] A host can be a member of more than one multicast group at a time. How active a multicast group is and what members it has can vary from group to group and from time to time. A multicast group can be active for a long time, or it can be very short-lived. Membership in a group can constantly change. A group that has members can have no activity.
[P6831|Normal] MLD packets are sent using these IPv6 multicast group addresses:
[P6832|Item List] MLD general queries are destined to the address ff02::1 (all systems on a subnet).
[P6833|Item List] MLD group-specific queries are destined to the group IPv6 address for which the switch is querying.
[P6834|Item List] MLD group membership reports are destined to the group IPv6 address for which the switch is reporting.
[P6835|Item List] MLD Version 1 (MLDv1) leave messages are destined to the address ff02::2 (all-multicast-routers on a subnet). In some old host IPv6 stacks, leave messages might be destined to the group IPv6 address rather than to the all-routers address.
[P6836|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6837|Normal] The MLD module is based on the following RFC
[P6838|Item List] RFC 2710
[P6839|Item List] RFC 3810
[P6840|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6841|Normal] There is no explicit command to enable MLD, which is always combined with PIMv6-SM. When PIMv6-SM is enabled on an interface, MLD will be enabled automatically on this interface, vice versa. But notice, before MLD can work, IPv6 Multicast-routing must be enabled globally firstly. We support build MLD group record by learning MLD packets or configuring static MLD group by administer.
[P6842|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6843|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6844|Heading 5] step 2 Enable ipv6 and ipv6 multicast-routing globally
[P6845|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 enable
Switch(config)# ipv6 multicast-routing 
[P6846|Heading 5] step 3 Enter the interface configure mode, set the ipv6 address and enable pim sparse mode
[P6847|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport 
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:1::1/64
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 pim sparse-mode
[P6848|Heading 5] step 4 Configuring MLD Interface Parameters
[P6849|Terminal Display] Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld version 2 
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld query-interval 120
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld query-max-response-time 12
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld robustness-variable 3
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld last-member-query-count 3
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld last-member-query-interval 2000
[P6850|Heading 5] step 5 Limit Max MLD Group Number
[P6851|Normal] Set the maxinum of ipv6 mld on the interface:
[P6852|Terminal Display] Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld limit 1000
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6853|Normal] Set the maxinum of ipv6 mld globally:
[P6854|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 mld limit 2000
[P6855|Heading 5] step 6 Create static mld group
[P6856|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld static-group ff0e::1234
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6857|Heading 5] step 7 Set IPv6 MLD proxy (optional)
[P6858|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 pim sparse-mode 
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld proxy-service
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 pim sparse-mode 
Switch(config-if)# ipv6 mld mroute-proxy eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P6859|Heading 5] step 8 Exit the configure mode
[P6860|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P6861|Heading 5] step 9 Validation

[P6866|Heading 2] Configuring PIMv6-SM
[P6867|Heading 3] Overview
[P6868|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P6869|Normal] The Protocol Independent Multicasting-Sparse Mode for IPv6 (PIMv6-SM) is a multicast routing protocol designed to operate efficiently across Wide Area Networks (WANs) with sparsely distributed groups. It helps network nodes that are geographically dispersed to conserve bandwidth, and reduces traffic by simultaneously delivering a single stream of information to multiple locations.
[P6870|Body Text] PIMv6-SM uses the IPv6 multicast model of receiver-initiated membership, supporting both shared and shortest-path trees, and uses soft-state mechanisms to adapt to changing network conditions. It relies on a topology-gathering protocol to populate a multicast routing table with routes.
[P6871|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P6872|Normal] The PIMv6-SM module is based on the following IETF standard: RFC 4601
[P6873|Body Text] Terminology：
[P6874|Item List] Rendezvous Point (RP): A Rendezvous Point (RP) router is configured as the root of the non-source-specific distribution tree for a multicast group. Join messages from receivers for a group are sent towards the RP. Data from senders is sent to the RP so that receivers can discover who the senders are, and receive traffic destined for the group.
[P6875|Item List] Multicast Routing Information Base (MRIB): The MRIB is a multicast topology table derived from the unicast routing table. In PIMv6-SM, the MRIB is used to decide where to send Join/Prune messages. It also provides routing metrics for destination addresses. These metrics are used when sending and processing Assert messages.
[P6876|Item List] Reverse Path Forwarding: Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) is a concept of an optimized form of flooding, where the router accepts a packet from SourceA through Interface IF1 only if IF1 is the interface the router would use in order to reach SourceA. It determines whether the interface is correct by consulting its unicast routing tables. The packet that arrives through interface IF1 is forwarded because the routing table lists this interface as the shortest path to the network. The router’s unicast routing table determines the shortest path for the multicast packets. Because a router accepts a packet from only one neighbor, it floods the packet only once, meaning that (assuming point-to-point links) each packet is transmitted over each link once in each direction.
[P6877|Item List] Tree Information Base (TIB): The TIB is the collection of state at a PIM router storing the state of all multicast distribution trees at that router. It is created by receiving Join/Prune messages, Assert messages, and MLD information from local hosts.
[P6878|Item List] Upstream: Towards the root of the tree. The root of the tree might be either the Source or the RP.
[P6879|Item List] Downstream: Away from the root of the tree. The root of tree might be either the Source or the RP.
[P6880|Item List] Source-Based Trees: In the Source-Based Trees concept, the forwarding paths are based on the shortest unicast path to the source. If the unicast routing metric is hop counts, the branches of the multicast Source-Based Trees are minimum hop. If the metric is delay, the branches are minimum delay. For every multicast source, there is a corresponding multicast tree that directly connects the source to all receivers. All traffic to the members of an associated group passes along the tree made for their source. Source-Based Trees have two entries with a list of outgoing interfaces– the source address and the multicast group.
[P6881|Item List] Shared Trees: Shared trees or RP trees (RPT) rely on a central router called the Rendezvous Point (RP) that receives all traffic from the sources, and forwards that traffic to the receivers. All hosts might not be receivers. There is a single tree for each multicast group, regardless of the number of sources. Only the routers on the tree know about the group, and information is sent only to interested receivers. With an RP, receivers have a place to join, even if no source exists. The shared tree is unidirectional, and information flows only from the RP to the receivers. If a host other than the RP has to send data on the tree, the data must first be tunneled to the RP, and then multicast to the members. This means that even if a receiver is also a source, it can only use the tree to receive packets from the RP, and not to send packets to the RP (unless the source is located between the RP and the receivers).
[P6882|Item List] Bootstrap Router (BSR): When a new multicast sender starts sending data packets, or a new receiver starts sending the Join message towards the RP for that multicast group, it needs to know the next-hop router towards the RP. The BSR provides group-to-RP mapping information to all the PIMv6 routers in a domain, allowing them to map to the correct RP address.
[P6883|Item List] Sending out Hello Messages: PIMv6 routers periodically send Hello messages to discover neighboring PIMv6 routers. Hello messages are multicast using the address ff02::d (ALL-PIMv6-ROUTERS group). Routers do not send any acknowledgement that a Hello message was received. A hold time value determines the length of time for which the information is valid. In PIMv6-SM, a downstream receiver must join a group before traffic is forwarded on the interface.
[P6884|Item List] Electing a Designated Router: In a multi-access network with multiple routers connected, one of them is selected to act as a designated router (DR) for a given period of time. The DR is responsible for sending Join/Prune messages to the RP for local members.
[P6885|Item List] Determining the RP: PIMv6-SM uses a BootStrap Router (BSR) to originate Bootstrap messages, and to disseminate RP information. The messages are multicast to the group on each link. If the BSR is not apparent, the routers flood the domain with advertisements. The router with the highest priority (if priorities are same, the higher IPv6 address applies) is selected to be the RP. Routers receive and store Bootstrap messages originated by the BSR. When a DR gets a membership indication from MLD for (or a data packet from) a directly connected host, for a group for which it has no entry, the DR maps the group address to one of the candidate RPs that can service that group. The DR then sends a Join/Prune message towards that RP. In a small domain, the RP can also be configured statically.
[P6886|Item List] Joining the Shared Tree: To join a multicast group, a host sends an MLD message to its upstream router, after which the router can accept multicast traffic for that group. The router sends a Join message to its upstream PIMv6 neighbor in the direction of the RP. When a router receives a Join message from a downstream router, it checks to see if a state exists for the group in its multicast routing table. If a state already exists, the Join message has reached the shared tree, and the interface from which the message was received is entered in the Outgoing Interface list. If no state exists, an entry is created, the interface is entered in the Outgoing Interface list, and the Join message is again sent towards the RP.
[P6887|Item List] Registering with the RP: A DR can begin receiving traffic from a source without having a Source or a Group state for that source. In this case, the DR has no information on how to get multicast traffic to the RP through a tree. When the source DR receives the initial multicast packet, it encapsulates it in a Register message, and unicasts it to the RP for that group. The RP decapsulates each Register message, and forwards the extracted data packet to downstream members on the RPT. Once the path is established from the source to the RP, the DR begins sending traffic to the RP as standard IPv6 multicast packets, as well as encapsulated within Register messages. The RP temporarily receives packets twice. When the RP detects the normal multicast packets, it sends a Register-Stop message to the source DR, meaning it should stop sending register packets.
[P6888|Item List] Sending Register-Stop Messages: When the RP begins receiving traffic from the source, both as Register messages and as unencapsulated IPv6 packets, it sends a Register-Stop message to the DR. This notifies the DR that the traffic is now being received as standard IPv6 multicast packets on the SPT. When the DR receives this message, it stops encapsulating traffic in Register messages.
[P6889|Item List] Pruning the Interface: Routers attached to receivers send Prune messages to the RP to disassociate the source from the RP. When an RP receives a Prune message, it no longer forwards traffic from the source indicated in the Prune message. If all members of a multicast group are pruned, the MLD state of the DR is deleted, and the interface is removed from the Source and Group lists of the group.
[P6890|Item List] Forwarding Multicast Packets: PIMv6-SM routers forward multicast traffic onto all interfaces that lead to receivers that have explicitly joined a multicast group. Messages are sent to a group address in the local subnetwork, and have a Time to Live (TTL) of 1. The router performs an RPF check, and forwards the packet. Traffic that arrives on the correct interface is sent onto all outgoing interfaces that lead to downstream receivers if the downstream router has sent a join to this router, or is a member of this group.
[P6891|Heading 3] Configuration
[P6892|Heading 4] Configuring General PIMv6 Sparse-mode ( With static RP)
[P6893|Normal] PIMv6-SM is a soft-state protocol. The main requirement is to enable PIMv6-SM on desired interfaces, and configure the RP information correctly, through static or dynamic methods. All multicast group states are maintained dynamically as the result of MLD Report/Leave and PIMv6 Join/Prune messages. Currently, we support only one RP for all multicast groups (ff00::/8).
[P6894|Body Text] This section provides PIMv6-SM configuration examples for two relevant scenarios.
[P6895|Body Text] In this example, using the above topology, Switch1 is the Rendezvous Point (RP), and all routers are statically configured with RP information. While configuring the RP, make sure that:
[P6896|Item List] Every router includes the ipv6 pim rp-address 2001:1::1 statement, even if it does not have any source or group member attached to it.
[P6897|Item List] There is only one RP address for a group scope in the PIMv6 domain.
[P6898|Item List] All interfaces running PIMv6-SM must have sparse-mode enabled.
[P6899|Normal] 
[P6900|Figure Description] PIMv6 Sparse-mode

Switch(config)# ipv6 multicast-routing

[P6935|Heading 4] Configuring General PIMv6 Sparse-mode ( With dynamic RP)
[P6936|Normal] A static configuration of RP works for a small, stable PIMv6 domain; however, it is not practical for a large and not-suitable internet work. In such a network, if the RP fails, the network administrator might have to change the static configurations on all PIMv6 routers. Another reason for choosing dynamic configuration is a higher routing traffic leading to a change in the RP.
[P6937|Body Text] We use the BSR mechanism to dynamically maintain the RP information. For configuring RP dynamically in the above scenario, Switch1 on eth-0-1 and Switch2 on eth-0-9 are configured as Candidate RP using the ipv6 pim rp candidate command. Switch2 on eth-0-9 is also configured as Candidate BSR. Since no other router has been configured as Candidate BSR, the Switch2 becomes the BSR router, and is responsible for sending group-to-RP mapping information to all other routers in this PIMv6 domain.
[P6938|Body Text] The following output displays the complete configuration at Switch1 and Switch2.
[P6939|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P6940|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P6941|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P6942|Heading 5] step 2 Enable IPv6 & IPv6 multicast globally

[P6975|Heading 4] Configuring Boostrap Router
[P6976|Body Text] Every PIMv6 multicast group needs to be associated with the IPv6 address of a Rendezvous Point (RP). This address is used as the root of a group-specific distribution tree whose branches extend to all nodes in the domain that want to receive traffic sent to the group. For all senders to reach all receivers, all routers in the domain use the same mappings of group addresses to RP addresses. In order to determine the RP for a multicast group, a PIMv6 router maintains a collection of group-to-RP mappings, called the RP-Set.
[P6977|Body Text] The Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism for the class of multicast routing protocols in the PIMv6 domain use the concept of a Rendezvous Point as a means for receivers to discover the sources that send to a particular multicast group. The BSR mechanism is one way that a multicast router can learn the set of group-to-RP mappings required in order to function.
[P6978|Body Text] Some of the PIMv6 routers within a PIMv6 domain are configured as Candidate-RPs (C-RPs). A subset of the C-RPs will eventually be used as the actual RPs for the domain. An RP configured with a lower value in the priority field has higher a priority.
[P6979|Body Text] Some of the PIMv6 routers in the domain are configured to be Candidate-BSRs (C-BSRs). One of these C-BSRs is elected to be the bootstrap router (BSR) for the domain, and all PIMv6 routers in the domain learn the result of this election through BSM (Bootstrap messages). The C-BSR with highest value in priority field is Elected-BSR.
[P6980|Body Text] The C-RPs then reports their candidacy to the elected BSR, which chooses a subset of the C-RPs and distributes corresponding group-to-RP mappings to all the routers in the domain through Bootstrap messages.
[P6981|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.

[P7018|Heading 2] Configuring PIMv6-DM
[P7019|Heading 3] Overview
[P7020|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7021|Normal] The Ipv6 Protocol Independent Multicasting-Dense Mode (PIMv6-DM) is a multicast routing protocol designed to operate efficiently across Wide Area Networks (WANs) with densely distributed groups. It helps network nodes that are geographically dispersed to conserve bandwidth, and reduces traffic by simultaneously delivering a single stream of information to multiple locations.
[P7022|Body Text] PIMv6-DM assumes that when a source starts sending, all down stream systems want to receive multicast datagrams. Initially, multicast datagrams are flooded to all areas of the network. PIMv6-DM uses RPF to prevent looping of multicast datagrams while flooding. If some areas of the network do not have group members, PIMv6-DM will prune off the forwarding branch by instantiating prune state.
[P7023|Body Text] Prune state has a finite lifetime. When that lifetime expires, data will again be forwarded down the previously pruned branch. Prune state is associated with an (S,G) pair. When a new member for a group G appears in a pruned area, a router can “graft” toward the source S for the group, thereby turning the pruned branch back into a forwarding branch.
[P7024|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7025|Normal] The PIMv6-DM module is based on the following IETF standard: RFC 3973
[P7026|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7027|Heading 4] Configuring General PIM dense-mode
[P7028|Normal] PIMv6-DM is a soft-state protocol. The main requirement is to enable PIMv6-DM on desired interfaces. All multicast group states are maintained dynamically as the result of MLD Report/Leave and PIMv6 messages.
[P7029|Normal]

[P7062|Heading 2] Configuring MLD Snooping
[P7063|Heading 3] Overview
[P7064|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7065|Normal] Layer 2 switches can use MLD snooping to constrain the flooding of multicast traffic by dynamically configuring Layer 2 interfaces so that multicast traffic is forwarded only to those interfaces associated with IPv6 multicast devices. As the name implies, MLD snooping requires the LAN switch to snoop on the MLD transmissions between the host and the router and to keep track of multicast groups and member ports. When the switch receives an MLD report from a host for a particular multicast group, the switch adds the host port number to the forwarding table entry; when it receives an MLD Leave Group message from a host, it removes the host port from the table entry. It also deletes entries per entry if it does not receive MLD membership reports from the multicast clients. The multicast router sends out periodic general queries to all VLANs. All hosts interested in this multicast traffic send report and are added to the forwarding table entry. The switch forwards only one report per IPv6 multicast group to the multicast router. It creates one entry per VLAN in the Layer 2 forwarding table for each MAC group from which it receives an MLD report.
[P7066|Body Text] Layer 2 multicast groups learned through MLD snooping are dynamic. If you specify group membership for a multicast group address statically, your setting supersedes any automatic manipulation by MLD snooping. Multicast group membership lists can consist of both user-defined and MLD snooping-learned settings.
[P7067|Body Text] Limitations And Configuration Guideline
[P7068|Body Text] VRRP, RIPng and OSPFv3 used multicast IPv6 address, so you need to avoid use such multicast IPv6 addresses, which have same multicast MAC address with multicast IPv6 address reserved by VRRP, RIPng and OSPFv3.
[P7069|Item List] VRRP used multicast group address ff02::12, so when mld snooping and VRRP are working, you need to avoid using multicast group address that matched same mac address with group address ff02::12.
[P7070|Item List] OSPFv3 used multicast group address ff02::5, so when mld snooping and OSFPv3 are working, you need to avoid using multicast group address that matched same mac address with group address ff02::5.
[P7071|Item List] RIPng used multicast group address ff02::9, so when mld snooping and RIPng are working, you need to avoid using multicast group address that matched same mac address with group address ff02::9.
[P7072|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7073|Normal] N/A

[P7086|Heading 4] Configuring Fast Leave
[P7087|Normal] When MLD Snooping fast leave is enabled, the mld snooping group will be removed at once upon receiving a corresponding mld report. Otherwise the switch will send out specified mld specific query, if it doesn’t get response in specified period, it will remove the group. By default, mld snooping fast-leave is disabled globally and per vlan.

[P7098|Heading 4] Configuring Querier Parameters (optional)
[P7099|Normal] In order for MLD, and thus MLD snooping, to function, a multicast router must exist on the network and generate MLD queries. The tables created for snooping (holding the member ports for each multicast group) are associated with the querier. Without a querier the tables are not created and snooping will not work.

Switch(config)# ipv6 mld snooping query-max-response-time 5

[P7115|Heading 4] Configuring Mrouter Port
[P7116|Normal] An MLD Snooping mrouter port is a switch port which is assumed to connect a multicast router. The mrouter port is configured on the vlan or learnt dynamicly. When MLD general query packet or PIMv6 hello packet is received on port of specified VLAN, this port becomes mrouter port of this vlan. All the mld queries received on this port will be flooded on the belonged vlan. All the mld reports and leaves received on this vlan will be forwarded to the mrouter port, directly or aggregated, depending on the report-suppression configuration. In addition, all the multicast traffic on this vlan will be forwarded to this mrouter port.

[P7141|Heading 4] Configuring Report Suppression
[P7142|Normal] The switch uses MLD report suppression to forward only one MLD report per multicast router query to multicast devices. When MLD router suppression is enabled (the default), the switch sends the first MLD report from all hosts for a group to all the multicast routers. The switch does not send the remaining MLD reports for the group to the multicast routers. This feature prevents duplicate reports from being sent to the multicast devices.
[P7143|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7144|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7145|Heading 5] step 2 Enable mld snooping report suppression globally
[P7146|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 mld snooping report-suppression
[P7147|Heading 5] step 3 Enable mld snooping report suppression for a vlan
[P7148|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ipv6 mld snooping vlan 1 report-suppression
[P7149|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P7150|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end

[P7165|Heading 2] Configuring MVR6
[P7166|Heading 3] Overview
[P7167|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7168|Normal] Multicast VLAN Registration for IPv6 (MVR6) is designed for applications using wide-scale deployment of IPv6 multicast traffic across an Ethernet ring-based service provider network (for example, the broadcast of IPv6 multiple television channels over a service-provider network). MVR6 allows a subscriber on a port to subscribe and unsubscribe to an IPv6 multicast stream on the network-wide multicast VLAN. It allows the single multicast VLAN to be shared in the network while subscribers remain in separate VLANs. MVR6 provides the ability to continuously send IPv6 multicast streams in the multicast VLAN, but to isolate the streams from the subscriber VLANs for bandwidth and security reasons.
[P7169|Body Text] MVR6 assumes that subscriber ports subscribe and unsubscribe (join and leave) these multicast streams by sending out MLD join and leave messages. These messages can originate from an MLD version-1-compatible host with an Ethernet connection. Although MVR6 operates on the underlying mechanism of MLD snooping, the two features operation affect with each other. One can be enabled or disabled with affecting the behavior of the other feature. If MLD snooping and MVR6 are both enabled, MVR6 reacts only to join and leave messages from IPv6 multicast groups configured under MVR6. The switch CPU identifies the MVR6 IPv6 multicast streams and their associated MAC addresses in the switch forwarding table, intercepts the MLD messages, and modifies the forwarding table to include or remove the subscriber as a receiver of the multicast stream, and the receivers must be in a different VLAN from the source. This forwarding behavior selectively allows traffic to cross between different VLANs.
[P7170|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7171|Normal] 
[P7172|Figure Description] MVR6

[P7196|Heading 1] VPN Configuration Guide
[P7197|Heading 2] Configuring VPN
[P7198|Heading 3] Overview
[P7199|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7200|Normal] VPN is defined as a collection of sites sharing a common routing table. A customer site is connected to the service provider network by one or more interfaces, where the service provider associates each interface with a VPN routing table. A VPN routing table is called a VPN routing and forwarding (VRF) table. Beginning in privileged EXEC mode, follow these steps to configure one or more VRFs.
[P7201|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7202|Normal] N/A
[P7203|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7204|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7205|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7206|Heading 5] step 2 Create a vrf instance
[P7207|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip vrf vpn1
Switch(config-vrf)# rd 100:1
Switch(config-vrf)# router-id 1.1.1.1
Switch(config-vrf)# route-target both 100:1
Switch(config-vrf)# import map route-map
[P7208|Normal]  Enter either an AS system number
[P7209|Heading 5] step 3 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P7210|Terminal Display] Switch(config-vrf)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# no switch
Switch(config-if)# ip vrf forwarding vpn1
Switch(config-if)# ip add 1.1.1.1/24
Switch(config-if)# end
[P7211|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P7212|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end

[P7216|Heading 2] Configuring IPv4 GRE Tunnel
[P7217|Heading 3] Overview
[P7218|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7219|Normal] Tunneling is an encapsulation technology, which uses one network protocol to encapsulate packet of another network protocol and transfer them over a virtual point to point connection. The virtual connection is called a tunnel. Tunneling refers to the whole process from data encapsulation to data transfer to data de-encapsulation.
[P7220|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7221|Normal] 
[P7222|Figure Description] IPv4 gre over IPv4
[P7223|Body Text] When it is required to communicate with isolated IPv4 networks, you should create a tunnel mechanism between them. The tunnel with transmit protocol of gre connected with two isolated IPv4 island is called IPv4 gre tunnel, which is that IPv4 packets are encapsulated by gre protocol over outer IPv4 packets. Gre tunnel would add gre head in encapsulated packets, including key, sequence, checksum and so on. In order to make an implement of gre tunnel, both tunnel endpoints must support the IPv4 protocol stacks.
[P7224|Body Text] IPv4 gre tunnel processes packets in the following ways:
[P7225|Item List] A host in the IPv4 network sends an IPv4 packet to Switch1 at the tunnel source.
[P7226|Item List] After determining according to the routing table that the packet needs to be forwarded through the tunnel, Switch1 encapsulates the IPv4 packet with an IPv4 header and forwards it through the physical interface of the tunnel.
[P7227|Item List] Upon receiving the packet, Switch2 de-encapsulates the packet.
[P7228|Item List] Switch2 forwards the packet according to the destination address in the de-encapsulated IPv4 packet. If the destination address is the device itself, Switch2 forwards the IPv4 packet to the upper-layer protocol for processing. In the process of de-encapsulation, it would check gre key, only the matched key of packet can be processed, otherwise discarded.
[P7229|Normal] The ip address of tunnel source and tunnel destination is manually assigned, and it provides point-to-point connection. By using overlay tunnels, you can communicate with isolated IPv4 networks without upgrading the IPv4 infrastructure between them. Overlay tunnels can be configured between border routers or between border routers and a host.
[P7230|Body Text] The primary use is for stable connections that require regular secure communication between two edge routers or between an end system and an edge router, or for connection to remote IPv4 networks, gre key is alternative configuration.
[P7231|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7232|Normal] 
[P7233|Figure Description] IPv4 gre Tunnel
[P7234|Body Text] As the topology shows, two IPv4 networks connect to the network via Switch1 and Switch2. An Ipv4 gre tunnel is required between Switch1 and Switch2, in order to connect two networks.
[P7235|Body Text] A reachable Ipv4 route is necessary for forwarding tunnel packet. Ipv4 address must be configured on tunnel interface; otherwise the route via this tunnel interface is invalid.
[P7236|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P7237|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7238|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7239|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P7240|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch1:
[P7241|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1/24
Switch(config-if)# tunnel enable
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.168.11.1/24
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7242|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch2:
[P7243|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1/24
Switch(config-if)# tunnel enable
Switch(config-if)# exit
    
Switch(config)# interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-if)# no switchport
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.1/24
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7244|Heading 5] step 3 Configure the tunnel interface
[P7245|Normal] Tunnel interface configuration for Switch1:
[P7246|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface tunnel1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel mode gre
Switch(config-if)# tunnel source eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel destination 192.168.20.1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel gre key 100
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.192.168.1/24
Switch(config-if)# keepalive 5 3
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7247|Normal] Tunnel interface configuration for Switch2:
[P7248|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface tunnel1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel mode gre
Switch(config-if)# tunnel source eth-0-1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel destination 192.168.10.1
Switch(config-if)# tunnel gre key 100
Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.192.168.2/24
Switch(config-if)# keepalive 5 3
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7249|Heading 5] step 4 Configure the static route and arp
[P7250|Normal] Configuring Switch1:
[P7251|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0/24 192.168.10.2
Switch(config)# ip route 192.168.12.0/24 tunnel1

Switch(config)# ip route 192.168.11.0/24 tunnel1

[P7263|Heading 1] Reliability Configuration Guide
[P7264|Heading 2] Configuring BHM
[P7265|Heading 3] Overview
[P7266|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7267|Normal] BHM is a module which is used to monitor other Processes. When a monitored Process is uncontrolled, the BHM module will take measures, such as printing warning on screen, shutting all ports, or restarting the system, to help or remind users to recover the system.
[P7268|Body Text] The monitored Processes include RIP, RIPNG, OSPF, OSPF6, BGP, LDP, RSVP, PIM, PIM6, 802.1X, LACP MSTP, DHCP-RELAY, DHCP-RELAY6, RMON, OAM, ONM, SSH, SNMP, PTP, SSM. In addition, some system procedures are also monitored, including NSM, IMI, CHSM, HSRVD. There are three activations of BHM, including “reload system”, including “reload system”,“warning”, “shutdown port”.
[P7269|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7270|Normal] N/A
[P7271|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7272|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7273|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7274|Heading 5] step 2 Enable system monitor and heart-beat-monitor globally
[P7275|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# sysmon enable
Switch(config)# heart-beat-monitor enable
[P7276|Heading 5] step 3 Reload system if a monitored PM is uncontrolled
[P7277|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# heart-beat-monitor reactivate reload system
[P7278|Normal] There are three activations of BHM, including “reload system”,“warning”, “shutdown port”.
[P7279|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P7280|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7281|Heading 5] step 5 Validation
[P7282|Terminal Display] Switch# show heart-beat-monitor
heart-beat-monitor enable.
heart-beat-monitor reactivation: restart system.
[P7283|Heading 3] Application cases
[P7284|Normal] N/A
[P7285|Heading 2] Configuring EFM OAM
[P7286|Heading 3] Overview
[P7287|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7288|Normal] This chapter contains a complete sample EFM OAM configuration. To see details on the commands used in this example, or to see the outputs of the validation commands, refer to the OAM Command Reference. To avoid repetition, some Common commands, like configure terminal, have not been listed under the commands used sections.
[P7289|Body Text] The main functions of Ethernet to the First Mile - Operation Administration and Maintenance (EFM-OAM) are link performance monitoring, fault detection, fault signaling and loopback signaling. OAM information is conveyed in Slow Protocol frames called OAM Protocol Data Units (OAMPDUs). OAMPDUs contain the appropriate control and status information used to monitor, test and troubleshoot OAM-enabled links.
[P7290|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7291|Normal] Reference: IEEE 802.3ah (2004)
[P7292|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7293|Heading 4] Configuring Enable EFM
[P7294|Normal] 
[P7295|Figure Description] EFM
[P7296|Body Text] The following configurations are same on Switch1 and Switch2.
[P7297|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7298|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7299|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and enable ethernet oam
[P7300|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam enable
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam mode active
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam link-monitor frame threshold high 10 window 50
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7301|Normal] ethernet oam mode can be “active” or “passive”. For example:
[P7302|Terminal Display] Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam mode passive 
[P7303|Normal] At least one switch among Switch1 and Switch2 should use mode active. Both switch use active can also work normally.
[P7304|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P7305|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7306|Heading 5] step 5 Validation
[P7307|Normal] The EFM Discovery Machine State should be “send any” in both machines. This is the expected normal operating state for OAM on fully-operational links.
[P7308|Body Text] The various states of OAM discovery state machine are defined below.
[P7309|Item List] ACTIVE_SEND_LOCAL: A DTE configured in Active mode sends Information OAMPDUs that only contain the Local Information TLV. This state is called ACTIVE_SEND_LOCAL. While in this state, the local DTE waits for Information OAMPDUs received from the remote DTE.
[P7310|Item List] PASSIVE_WAIT: DTE configured in Passive mode waits until receiving Information OAMPDUs with Local Information TLVs before sending any Information OAMPDUs with Local Information TLVs. This state is called PASSIVE_WAIT. By waiting until first receiving an Information OAMPDU with the Local Information TLV, a Passive DTE cannot complete the OAM Discovery process when connected to another Passive DTE.
[P7311|Item List] SEND_LOCAL_REMOTE: Once the local DTE has received an Information OAMPDU with the Local Information TLV from the remote DTE, the local DTE begins sending Information OAMPDUs that contain both the Local and Remote Information TLVs. This state is called SEND_LOCAL_REMOTE.
[P7312|Item List] SEND_LOCAL_REMOTE_OK: If the local OAM client deems the settings on both the local and remote DTEs are acceptable, it enters the SEND_LOCAL_REMOTE_OK state.
[P7313|Item List] SEND_ANY: Once an OAMPDU has been received indicating the remote device is satisfied with the respective settings, the local device enters the SEND_ANY state. This is the expected normal operating state for OAM on fully operational links.
[P7314|Item List] FAULT: If OAM is reset, disabled, or the link timer expires, the Discovery process returns to the FAULT state.

[P7319|Heading 4] Configuring Remote Loopback
[P7320|Normal] 
[P7321|Figure Description] EFM
[P7322|Body Text] OAM remote loopback can be used for fault localization and link performance testing. In addition, an implementation may analyze loopback frames within the OAM sublayer to determine additional information about the health of the link (i.e. determine which frames are being dropped due to link errors).
[P7323|Body Text] The following configurations are same on Switch1 and Switch2 if there is no special description.
[P7324|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7325|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7326|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and enable ethernet oam remote loopback
[P7327|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam enable
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam remote loopback supported
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7328|Heading 5] step 3 Exit the configure mode
[P7329|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7330|Heading 5] step 4 Start remote loopback
[P7331|Normal] Configure on Switch1:
[P7332|Terminal Display] Switch# ethernet oam remote-loopback start interface eth-0-9
[P7333|Heading 5] step 5 Validation
[P7334|Normal] Display results on Switch1:
[P7335|Terminal Display] Switch# show ethernet oam state-machine interface eth-0-9
State Machine Details:
--------------------------------

Local OAM enable:                        Enable

Local pdu status:                           ANY 
Local Satisfied:                            True 
Local Stable:                               True 
Remote Satisfied valid:                     True 
Remote Stable:                             True 
Local Parser State:                         Discard
Local Multiplexer State:                     Forward
Remote Parser State:                        Loopback
Remote Multiplexer State:                   Discard
[P7336|Heading 4] Configuring Link Monitoring Event
[P7337|Normal] 
[P7338|Figure Description] EFM
[P7339|Body Text] We can configure high and low threshold for link-monitoring features. We can also configure an error disable action if one of the high thresholds is exceeded.
[P7340|Body Text] The following configurations and validations are operated on Switch1:
[P7341|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7342|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7343|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and set the threshold for error packetes
[P7344|Terminal Display] Switch(config)#interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam link-monitor frame threshold high 5000 low 200 window 500
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam link-monitor frame-seconds threshold high 600 low 200 window 9000
[P7345|Normal]  The “ethernet oam link-monitor frame threshold” command specifies the high and low thresholds of error packets in a period. The period is defined by arguments “window 500”, the unit is 100 millisecond, the default value is 1 second. In this case the high threshold is 5000 packets and the low threshold is 200 packets.
[P7346|Body Text] The “ethernet oam link-monitor frame-seconds threshold” command specifies the high and low thresholds of the seconds which have error packets in a period. The period is defined by arguments “window 9000”, the unit is 100 millisecond, the default value is 100 second. In this case the high threshold is 600 seconds and the low threshold is 200 seconds.
[P7347|Heading 5] step 3 Set the action when reach the threshold
[P7348|Normal] When the error packets exceed the threshold configured in step 2, set the interface status to error-disable
[P7349|Terminal Display] Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam link-monitor high-threshold action error-disable-interface
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7350|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P7351|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7352|Heading 5] step 5 Validation
[P7353|Terminal Display] Switch#show ethernet oam status interface eth-0-9

[P7354|Heading 4] Configuring Remote Failure Detection
[P7355|Normal] 
[P7356|Figure Description] EFM
[P7357|Body Text] An error-disable action can be configured to occur on an interface so that if any of the critical link events (link fault, dying gasp, etc.) occurs in the remote machine, the interface is shut down.
[P7358|Body Text] The following configurations and validations are operated on Switch1:
[P7359|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7360|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7361|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and set action when the remote link failure
[P7362|Terminal Display] Switch(config)#interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# ethernet oam remote-failure critical-event dying-gasp link-fault action error-disable-interface
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7363|Heading 5] step 3 Exit the configure mode
[P7364|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7365|Heading 2] Configuring CFM
[P7366|Heading 3] Overview
[P7367|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7368|Normal] CFM = Connectivity Fault Management
[P7369|Body Text] CFM provides the capability to detect, verify, isolate and notify connectivity failures on a Virtual Bridged LAN based on the protocol standard specified in IEEE 802.1ag. It provides for discovery and verification of paths through 802.1 bridges and LANs, and is part of the enhanced Operation, Administration and Management (OAM) features. CFM is designed to be transparent to the customer data transported by a network and to be capable of providing maximum fault coverage.
[P7370|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7371|Normal] Reference: IEEE 802.1ag/D8.1
[P7372|Body Text] CFM uses standard Ethernet frames distinguished by EtherType. These CFM messages are supported:
[P7373|Heading 5] Continuity Check messages (CC)
[P7374|Normal] Multicast heartbeat messages exchanged periodically between MEPs that allow MEPs to discover other MEPs within a domain and allow MIPs to discover MEPs. It is used to detect loss of continuity (LOC) between any pair of MEPs.
[P7375|Heading 5] Loopback messages
[P7376|Normal] Unicast frames transmitted by an MEP at administrator request to verify connectivity to a particular maintenance point, indicating if a destination is reachable. A loopback message is similar to an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) ping message.
[P7377|Heading 5] Linktrace messages
[P7378|Normal] Multicast frames transmitted by an MEP at administrator request to track the path (hop-by-hop) to a destination MEP/MIP. Traceroute messages are similar in concept to UDP traceroute messages.
[P7379|Heading 5] Delay Measurement messages
[P7380|Normal] A MEP sends DMM with ETH-DM request information to its peer MEP and receives DMR with ETH-DM reply information from its peer MEP to carry out two-way frame delay and delay variation measurements.
[P7381|Body Text] When a MEP receives 1DM frames, it will carry out one-way frame delay and delay variation measurements.
[P7382|Heading 5] Ethernet Locked Signal messages
[P7383|Normal] Ethernet Locked Signal function (ETH-LCK) is used to communicate the administrative locking of a server (sub) layer MEP and consequential interruption of data traffic forwarding towards the MEP expecting this traffic. It allows a MEP receiving frames with ETH-LCK information to differentiate between a defect condition and an administrative locking action at the server (sub) layer MEP.
[P7384|Heading 5] Ethernet client signal fail messages
[P7385|Normal] The Ethernet client signal fail function (ETH-CSF) is used by a MEP to propagate to a peer MEP the detection of a failure or defect event in an Ethernet client signal when the client itself does not support appropriate fault or defect detection or propagation mechanisms, such as ETH-CC or ETH-AIS. The ETH-CSF messages propagate in the direction from the Ethernet source-adaptation function detecting the failure or defect event to the Ethernet sink-adaptation function associated with the peer MEP. ETH-CSF is only applicable to point-to-point Ethernet transport applications.
[P7386|Heading 5] Ethernet Frame loss measurement message
[P7387|Normal] ETH-LM is used to collect counter values applicable for ingress and egress service frames where the counters maintain a count of transmitted and received data frames between a pair of MEPs.
[P7388|Body Text] ETH-LM is performed by sending LMM with ETH-LM information to a peer MEP and similarly receiving LMR with ETH-LM information from the peer MEP.
[P7389|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7390|Normal]  CFM is conflict with 802.1x and mirror destination on the same port. Therefore, CFM and these functions should not be configured on the same port.
[P7391|Heading 4] Configure CC/LB/LT/AIS/DM
[P7392|Normal] 
[P7393|Figure Description] CFM
[P7394|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P7395|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7396|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7397|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the vlan configure mode and create the vlan
[P7398|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# vlan database
Switch(config vlan)# vlan 30
Switch(config vlan)# exit
[P7399|Heading 5] step 3 Enable CFM globally and set cfm mode to y1731
[P7400|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm enable
Switch(config)# ethernet cfm mode y1731
[P7401|Heading 5] step 4 Create the cfm domain and bind the service with a vlan
[P7402|Normal] Create a domain which has the name “cust” and level 5.
[P7403|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm domain cust level 5
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# service cst vlan 30
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# exit
[P7404|Normal] Create a domain which has the name “provid” and level 3.
[P7405|Body Text] Configuring Switch2 and Switch3:
[P7406|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm domain provid level 3
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# service cst vlan 30
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# exit
[P7407|Normal]  The range of the cfm domain level should be 0-7. The larger number indicates the higher priority. When different cfm domains have the same vlan, the packets of the domain with higher priority can pass through the domains with lower priority.
[P7408|Heading 5] step 5 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P7409|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch1:
[P7410|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 66 domain cust vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep crosscheck mpid 99 domain cust vlan 30 mac d036.4567.8009
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7411|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch2:
[P7412|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mip level 5 vlan 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep up mpid 666 domain provid vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep crosscheck mpid 999 domain provid vlan 30 mac 6a08.051e.bd09
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm ais status enable all domain provid vlan 30 level 5 multicast
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm server-ais status enable level 5 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-17
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7413|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch3:
[P7414|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mip level 5 vlan 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep up mpid 999 domain provid vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep crosscheck mpid 666 domain provid vlan 30 mac 0e1d.a7d7.fb09
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
Switch(config)# interface eth-0-17
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7415|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch4:
[P7416|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 99 domain cust vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep crosscheck mpid 66 domain cust vlan 30 mac fa02.cdff.6a09
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7417|Heading 5] step 6 Enable continuity check
[P7418|Normal] Configuring Switch1 and Switch4:
[P7419|Terminal Display] Switch1(config)# ethernet cfm cc enable domain cust vlan 30
[P7420|Normal] Configuring Switch2 and Switch3:
[P7421|Terminal Display] Switch2(config)# ethernet cfm cc enable domain provid vlan 30
[P7422|Heading 5] step 7 Alarm configuration (optional)
[P7423|Normal] Suppress errors when ais packet is received and loc error.
[P7424|Body Text] Configuring Switch1:
[P7425|Terminal Display]  Switch(config)# ethernet cfm ais suppress alarm enable domain cust vlan 30
[P7426|Heading 5] step 8 Exit the configure mode
[P7427|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7428|Heading 5] step 9 Validation

[P7490|Heading 4] Configure CSF
[P7491|Normal] 
[P7492|Figure Description] CFM CSF
[P7493|Body Text] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P7494|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7495|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7496|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the vlan configure mode and create the vlan
[P7497|Normal] Configuring Switch1:
[P7498|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# vlan database
Switch(config vlan)# vlan 30
Switch(config vlan)# exit
[P7499|Normal] Configuring Switch2 and Switch3:
[P7500|Terminal Display] Switch3(config)# vlan database
Switch3(config vlan)# vlan 20,30
Switch3(config vlan)# exit
[P7501|Heading 5] step 3 Enable CFM globally and set cfm mode to y1731
[P7502|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm enable
Switch(config)# ethernet cfm mode y1731
[P7503|Heading 5] step 4 Create the cfm domain and bind the service with a vlan
[P7504|Normal] Create a domain which has the name “cust” and level 5.
[P7505|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm domain cust level 5
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# service cst vlan 30
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# exit
[P7506|Normal] Create a domain which has the name “provid” and level 3.
[P7507|Body Text] Configuring Switch2 and Switch3:
[P7508|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm domain provid level 3
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# service cst vlan 20
Switch(config-ether-cfm)# exit
[P7509|Heading 5] step 5 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P7510|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch1:
[P7511|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 66 domain cust vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep crosscheck mpid 99 domain cust vlan 30 mac d036.4567.8009
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7512|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch2:
[P7513|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 99 domain cust vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep crosscheck mpid 66 domain cust vlan 30 mac fa02.cdff.6a09
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)#interface eth-0-17
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 666 domain provid vlan 20 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown   
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7514|Normal] Interface configuration for Switch3:
[P7515|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 88 domain cust vlan 30 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)#interface eth-0-17
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
Switch(config-if)# ethernet cfm mep down mpid 999 domain provid vlan 20 interval 1
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7516|Heading 5] step 6 Enable continuity check
[P7517|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm cc enable domain cust vlan 30
[P7518|Heading 5] step 7 Configure csf relation between client mep and server mep
[P7519|Normal] Configuring Switch2:
[P7520|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm csf client domain cust vlan 30 mepid 99 server domain provid vlan 20 mepid 666 interval 1
[P7521|Normal] Configuring Switch3:
[P7522|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# ethernet cfm csf client domain cust vlan 30 mepid 88 server domain provid vlan 20 mepid 999 interval 1

[P7575|Heading 2] Configuring CPU Traffic
[P7576|Heading 3] Overview
[P7577|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7578|Normal] CPU traffic limit is a useful mechanism for protecting CPU from malicious flows by injecting huge volume of PDUs into switches.
[P7579|Body Text] CPU traffic limit provides two-level protection for CPU.
[P7580|Item List] The low-level traffic limit is performed for each reason, which is realized by queue shaping of each type of PDU.
[P7581|Item List] The high-level traffic limit is performed for all reasons, which is realized by channel shaping at CPU channel.
[P7582|Normal] With this two-level protection, each PDU-to-CPU rate is limited and the overall PDU-to-CPU rate is also limited.
[P7583|Body Text] ：The word “reason”, means this type of packets will be sent to cpu for further processing.
[P7584|Body Text] The description of all reason is as following.

[TABLE 19] rows=42 cols=2
R1	Reason	Description
R2	arp	Address Resolution Protocol
R3	bpdu	Bridge Protocol Data Unit
R4	dhcp	Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
R5	eapol	Extensible Authentication Protocol Over Lan
R6	erps	Ethernet Ring Protection Switching
R7	fwd-to-cpu	Packets forwarding to cpu
R8	icmp-redirect	ICMP Redirect
R9	igmp	IGMP Snooping Protocol
R10	ip-option	Packets with IP Option
R11	ipda	IP Destination to Router-self
R12	ssh	SSH protocol packet
R13	telnet	Telnet protocol packet
R14	mlag	MLAG protocol packet
R15	tcp	TCP protocol packet
R16	ldp	Label Distribution Protocol
R17	macsa-mismatch	Port Security for source mac learned
R18	mcast-rpf-fail	Multicast with rpf fail or first multicast packet
R19	mpls-ttl-fail	Mpls Packets with ttl fail
R20	ip-mtu-fail	IP packet with mtu fail
R21	ospf	Open Shortest Path First
R22	pim	Protocol Independent Multicast
R23	port-security-discard	Port Security for exceeding fdb maxnum
R24	rip	Routing Information Protocol
R25	sflow-egress	Sampled flow at egress direction
R26	sflow-ingress	Sampled flow at ingress direction
R27	slow-protocol	Slow Protocol (including EFM, LACP and SYNCE)
R28	smart-link	Smart Link Protocol
R29	ucast-ttl-fail	Unicast Packets with ttl fail
R30	udld	Unidirectional Link Detection Protocol
R31	vlan-security-discard	Vlan Security for exceeding fdb maxnum
R32	vrrp	Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol
R33	bfd-learning	BFD learning packets
R34	dot1x-mac-bypass	Mac auth bypass packets
R35	bgp	Border gateway protocol packet
R36	egress-ttl-fail	Egress ttl fail packet
R37	icmpv6	ICMPv6 packet
R38	l2protocol-tunnel	Layer2 protocol tunnel packet
R39	loopback-detection	lLoopback detection packet
R40	mirror-to-cpu	Mirror to cpu packet
R41	ndp	Neighbor discovery protocol packet
R42	tunnel-gre-keepalive	Tunnel gre keepalive reply packet

[P7589|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7590|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7591|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7592|Heading 5] step 2 Set the total rate
[P7593|Normal] The default value of total rate is 2000, the unit is pps (packet-per-second)
[P7594|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# cpu-traffic-limit total rate 3000
[P7595|Heading 5] step 3 Set the saparate rate
[P7596|Normal] Use RIP packets for example:
[P7597|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# cpu-traffic-limit reason rip rate 500
[P7598|Heading 5] step 4 Set the reason class
[P7599|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# cpu-traffic-limit reason rip class 3
[P7600|Normal]  The valid range of reason class is 0-3. The larger number indicates the higher priority.
[P7601|Heading 5] step 5 Exit the configure mode
[P7602|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end

[P7608|Heading 2] Configuring UDLD
[P7609|Heading 3] Overview
[P7610|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7611|Normal] The Unidirectional Link Detection protocol is a light-weight protocol that can be used to detect and disable one-way connections before they create dangerous situations such as Spanning Tree loops or other protocol malfunctions.
[P7612|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7613|Normal] N/A
[P7614|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7615|Normal] 
[P7616|Figure Description] UDLD
[P7617|Body Text] The following configurations are same on Switch1 and Switch2.
[P7618|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7619|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7620|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the interface configure mode and enable udld
[P7621|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# udld port
Switch(config-if)# exit
[P7622|Heading 5] step 3 Enable udld globally
[P7623|Terminal Display]  Switch(config)# udld enable
[P7624|Heading 5] step 4 Set the message interval (optional)
[P7625|Normal] If the message is not specified, use the default value: 15 seconds.
[P7626|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# udld message interval 10
[P7627|Heading 5] step 5 Exit the configure mode
[P7628|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
[P7629|Heading 5] step 6 Validation
[P7630|Normal] Display the result on Switch1.
[P7631|Terminal Display] Switch# show udld eth-0-9

[P7634|Heading 2] Configuring ERPS
[P7635|Heading 3] Overview
[P7636|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7637|Normal] ERPS technology increases the availability and robustness of Ethernet rings. In the event that a fiber cut occurs, ERPS converges in less than one second, often in less than 50 milliseconds.
[P7638|Body Text] The main idea is described as the following. ERPS operates by declaring an ERPS domain on a single ring. On that ring domain, one switch, or node, is designated the master node, while all other nodes are designated as transit nodes. One port of the master node is designated as the master node’s primary port to the ring; another port is designated as the master node’s secondary port to the ring. In normal operation, the master node blocks the secondary port for all non-ERPS traffic belonging to this ERPS domain, thereby avoiding a loop in the ring. Keep-alive messages are sent by the master node in a pre-set time interval. Transit nodes in the ring domain will forward the ERPS messages. Once a link failure event occurs, the master node will detect this either by receiving the link-down message sent by the node adjacent to the failed link or by the timeout of the keep-alive message. After link failure is detected, master node will open the secondary port for data traffic to re-route the traffic.
[P7639|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7640|Normal] Reference: RFC 3619
[P7641|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7642|Normal] ERPS is a soft-state protocol. The main requirement is to enable ERPS on desired devices, and configure the ERPS information correctly for various network topologies.
[P7643|Body Text] This section provides ERPS configuration examples for their typical network topologies.
[P7644|Heading 4] Configuring ERPS for a Single-Ring Topology
[P7645|Normal] 
[P7646|Figure Description] ERPS
[P7647|Body Text] Configure same ERPS domain and ring at Switch1, Switch2 and Switch3. Switch1 is configured as ERPS master node and other two switches are configured as ERPS transit nodes. Interface agg11, which has two members called eth-0-9 and eth-0-10, is configured as primary interface at Switch1 and eth-0-13 is configured as secondary interface.
[P7648|Body Text]  The ports accessing an ERPS ring must be configured as trunk ports, permitting the traffic of data VLANs to pass through. If the switch is enabled stacking, the port of ERPS ring should not on slave stacking device.
[P7649|Item List] The ports accessing an ERPS ring must be configured as the members of the control VLAN, allowing the ERPS packets to be sent and received.
[P7650|Item List] STP on ports accessing ERPS rings must be disabled.
[P7651|Item List] Only one node can be configured as master node.
[P7652|Item List] Control VLAN must not be configured as Layer 3 interface.
[P7653|Item List] VLAN mapping must not be enabled on the ERPS ports.
[P7654|Item List] Native VLAN of a port accessing an ERPS ring must not be set as the primary control VLAN or the secondary control VLAN.
[P7655|Normal] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.
[P7656|Heading 5] step 1 Enter the configure mode
[P7657|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal
[P7658|Heading 5] step 2 Enter the vlan configure mode and create the vlan
[P7659|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# vlan database
Switch(config-vlan)# vlan 15
Switch(config-vlan)# exit
[P7660|Heading 5] step 3 Enter the interface configure mode and set the attributes of the interface
[P7661|Normal] As the topology shows，eth-0-9 and eth-0-10 of Switch1 and Switch2 join agg 11 and connect to each other directly. eth-0-13 of Switch1 and Switch3 connect to each other directly. eth-0-17 of Switch2 and Switch3 connect to each other directly.
[P7662|Body Text] Interface agg 11 configuration for Switch1 and Switch2:
[P7663|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface eth-0-9
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 15
Switch(config-if)# static-channel-group 11
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface eth-0-10
Switch(config-if)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 15
Switch(config-if)# static-channel-group 11
Switch(config-if)# exit

Switch(config)# interface agg11
Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree port disable

Switch(config-vlan)# exit

[P7717|Heading 3] Application cases
[P7718|Normal] N/A
[P7719|Heading 2] Configuring Smart Link
[P7720|Heading 3] Overview
[P7721|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7722|Normal] The Smart Link is a simple but practical technology of fast link protection. It is a solution specific to dual uplink networking to fulfill redundancy and fast migration of active and standby links.
[P7723|Body Text] Every smart-link group is included a pair of a layer 2 interfaces where one interface is configured to act as a standby to the other. The feature provides an alternative solution to the STP. Users can disable STP and still retain basic link redundancy. The feature also support load-balancing so than both interfaces simultaneously forward the traffic.
[P7724|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7725|Normal] N/A
[P7726|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7727|Normal] 
[P7728|Figure Description] Smart-Link Typical Topology
[P7729|Body Text] The figure above is a typical smart-link application. The Switch1 and Switch2 are configured smart-link group. Switch3, Switch4 and Switch5 are configured smart-link flush receiver.
[P7730|Body Text] To configure smart-link group, some configuration should be configured before it.
[P7731|Item List] VLANs should be configured.
[P7732|Item List] MSTP instance should be configured.
[P7733|Item List] Spanning-tree should be disabled in the interface.
[P7734|Item List] About above configurations, please see the related references.
[P7735|Normal] The following configuration should be operated on all switches if the switch ID is not specified.

Switch(config-mst)# instance 2 vlan 2
Switch(config-mst)# instance 3 vlan 3
[P7743|Terminal Display] Switch(config-mst)# instance 10 vlan 10

[P7778|Heading 2] Configuring Multi-Link
[P7779|Heading 3] Overview
[P7780|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7781|Normal] The Multi-Link is a simple but practical technology of fast link protection. It is a solution specific to multi-uplink networking to fulfill redundancy and fast migration of between links.
[P7782|Body Text] The feature is like smart link, but links extend to four instead of two.
[P7783|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7784|Normal] N/A
[P7785|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7786|Normal] 
[P7787|Figure Description] Multi-Link Typical Topology
[P7788|Body Text] The figure above is a typical multi-link application. The Switch1 are configured multi-link group. Switch2, Switch3, Switch4 and Switch5 are configured multi-link flush receiver.
[P7789|Body Text] To configure Multi-link group, some configuration should be configured before it.
[P7790|Item List] VLANs should be configured.
[P7791|Item List] MSTP instance should be configured.
[P7792|Item List] Spanning-tree should be disabled in the interface.
[P7793|Item List] About above configurations, please see the related references.

[P7817|Heading 4] Configuring Multi-Link Enhance
[P7818|Normal] There is an enhanced method to improve the ability of multi-link to protect link. When all the interfaces of multi-link group are down, you can enable another interface to send the enhance packet to peer which makes the instance state of one interface to change from block to active. It would avoid the switch being the state of islet.
[P7819|Body Text] When 2 multi-link group on different switches backup for each other, multi-link members on one switch is blocked and can not protect the traffic.
[P7820|Body Text] In this example:
[P7821|Item List] Core switch A and B, Access switch A and B, make up a full-match topology.
[P7822|Item List] Enable multi-link on Access switch A, the priority for link a/b/c is 1/2/3.
[P7823|Item List] Enable multi-link on Access switch B, the priority for link d/e is 1/2.
[P7824|Normal] In normal condition, link b/c/e are block, link a/d are active. As the following figure shows:
[P7825|Body Text] 
[P7826|Body Text] When link d/e are break down, the only out going link for Access switch B is link c, which is between Access switch A and Access switch B.
[P7827|Body Text] 
[P7828|Body Text] Because link c is blocked, the Access switch B is the state of islet. As the following figure shows:
[P7829|Normal] 
[P7830|Figure Description] Multilink-enhance Typical Topology
[P7831|Body Text] The figure above is a typical multi-link application. The Switch1, 2 are configured multi-link group. Switch1 has the interface which receives the multilink-enhance packets. And , Switch2 has the interface which sends the multilink-enhance packets.
[P7832|Body Text] To configure multi-link group, some configuration should be configured before it.
[P7833|Item List] VLANs should be configured.
[P7834|Item List] MSTP instance should be configured.
[P7835|Item List] Spanning-tree should be disabled in the interface.
[P7836|Item List] About above configurations, please see the related references.
[P7837|Item List] It should configure the control vlan and password of flush sending before setting the multilink-enhance interface.

[P7866|Heading 2] Configuring Monitor Link
[P7867|Heading 3] Overview
[P7868|Heading 4] Function Introduction
[P7869|Normal] Monitor Link is a port collaboration function. Monitor Link usually works together with Layer 2 topology protocols. The idea is to monitor the states of uplink ports and adapt the up/down state of downlink ports to the up/down state of uplink ports, triggering link switchover on the downstream switch in time.
[P7870|Heading 4] Principle Description
[P7871|Normal] N/A
[P7872|Heading 3] Configuration
[P7873|Normal] 
[P7874|Figure Description] monitor link

[P7876|Terminal Display] Switch# configure terminal

[P7878|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# interface range eth-0-1 - 3
Switch(config-if-range)# no shutdown
Switch(config-if-range)# exit
[P7879|Heading 5] step 3 Create multi link group and set the attributes of the group
[P7880|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# monitor-link group 1
Switch(config-mtlk-group)# monitor-link uplink interface eth-0-1
Switch(config-mtlk-group)# monitor-link downlink interface eth-0-2
Switch(config-mtlk-group)# monitor-link downlink interface eth-0-3
Switch(config-mtlk-group)# exit
[P7881|Heading 5] step 4 Exit the configure mode
[P7882|Terminal Display] Switch(config)# end
